#3574. Why Michael Stuhlbarg Left HBO's Boardwalk Empire

In "The Godfather Part II," Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) meets with the aged gangster Hyman Roth (Lee Strasberg) in his modest Florida home. Roth muses, "I've loved baseball ever since Arnold Rothstein fixed the World Series of 1919."

That reference isn't a movie embellishment. New York racketeer Arnold Rothstein really was alleged to have fixed the 1919 World Series in what's called "The Black Box Scandal," the blowback of which is explored in Season 1 of HBO's Prohibition period piece "Boardwalk Empire," featuring Michael Stuhlbarg as Rothstein. "AR," as his men often call him, remains a fixture of "Boardwalk Empire" during its first four seasons, and Stuhlbarg gives one of the show's standout performances.

Historians describe Rothstein as the one who put the "organized" in organized crime, thanks to a sharp knack for math and business. Stuhlbarg's Rothstein lives up to the history books. He's often shown playing pool or gambling and notes a great gambler never makes a bet without fixing the odds in his favor. He's extremely eloquent but only polite except in the most surface-level ways. Ice water runs in his veins.

So, it's a shame that he doesn't even get a real ending. History says that Rothstein died in 1928. "Boardwalk Empire" Season 4 ends in 1924, and then its fifth and final eight-episode season jumps ahead to 1931. That meant the show skips over lots of real history, including Rothstein's death. He simply disappears from the series, save for vague references to his demise in Season 5.

It's even more noticeable since his legacy hangs over the show's finale. "Boardwalk Empire" Season 5 includes a fictionalized account of how Rothstein's protégés "Lucky" Luciano (Vincent Piazza), Meyer Lansky (Anatol Yusef), and Benny "Bugsy" Siegel (Michael Zegen) took over the East Coast American mob.

Rothstein's death is a pretty big missing chapter in Season 5's story, but a consequence of the larger "Boardwalk Empire" production. Looking in from the outside, "Boardwalk Empire" appears to be a show that got cut short. A fifth and final season that's only two-thirds as long as the previous ones? And which leaps past several years of story? It's hard to believe that was always the intention. It really feels like a series that ran out of runway and jumped ahead to the intended ending to resolve itself as best it could. (Mind you, Season 5 still has some great episodes.)

The often repeated narrative is that "Boardwalk Empire" cost too much for HBO for too little a return, so it had to go. It was an unavoidably expensive show that came with a lot of homework for its cast (being a period piece), costing a reported $5 million per episode. The reported episode ratings do also show a consistent downward slump across seasons. From "Boardwalk Empire" Seasons 1-4, each successive season premiere and season finale was watched by fewer people than the previous one, and by Season 4, the show was slipping below even two million viewers an episode.

Nonetheless, "Boardwalk Empire" creator Terence Winter maintained back in 2014 that ending the series was a creative call. Speaking with Time and Hitflix, Winter said he and his writers felt series lead Nucky Thompson (Steve Buscemi) was already nearing his story's end by Season 4. 1931 was chosen as the most natural endpoint because it's when Al Capone (Stephen Graham) went to prison, Luciano and Lansky began the mafia's Commission, and Prohibition was winding down. The cost was skipping over major events like Rothstein's murder, which in real life remains shrouded in mystery.

Reportedly, Rothstein owed $300,000 after a poker loss and refused to pay up, earning him a bullet to the gut on November 4, 1928. But he took his killer's identity to the grave. Rothstein's real death being unsolved would give "Boardwalk Empire" dramatic license to fill in the details. I'm confident it would've pulled it off since whenever Rothstein was onscreen, "Boardwalk Empire" became a more compelling show.

The ending of "Boardwalk Empire" Season 4 even directly teases more to come from Rothstein. He enters a business alliance with Nucky's ex-wife, Margaret Thompson (a pre-"Lanterns" Kelly Macdonald), who is working as a secretary at a New York City investment firm and agrees to slip Rothstein insider information. Instead, nothing comes of that.

Stuhlbarg deserves a mountain's worth of credit. The actor studied his character, including how the real Rothstein thought of himself as a businessman and held his conduct to such a standard, and he's said the "Boardwalk Empire" writers' room was "amiable" about implementing his own research into his character. Stuhlbarg was similarly gracious about not returning for Season 5, especially considering it wasn't even his choice to leave the show, saying during a 2014 press junket that:

"They had to act fast, and they had a lot of ground to cover. It was amazing that we all got as much coverage as we did, considering how many characters they were juggling. I had so much fun doing the show, and I had no regrets. And yeah, sure it would've been fun to have shown [Rothstein's death], but I thought what they came up with was very cool, as it was. I think if they could have, they would've shown it, but they didn't have the time."

Ones of Matt Damon’s 2026 movie releases, The Odyssey, couldn’t stop breaking records after its debut this past July. It became the second highest-grossing movie of the year with a worldwide haul of $1.8 billion. It's also the highest-grossing R-rated movie ever and the 11th highest-grossing movie ever. At present, Damon's name is also being mentioned amid awards season conversations. Still, as the star comes off his big year, he's speaking honestly about what he considers to be the low points of his career.

The Good Will Hunting star was recently asked when he knew The Odyssey would be a hit, and he admitted that moment came when he saw the movie for himself. Decades earlier, Damon had those same instincts, as he explained to GQ. However, in those cases, the results weren't nearly as strong as they are now. While discussing one particular slump, Damon named one of the films he had on the docket in 2000:

The first time was before The Bourne Identity came out. I had done The Legend of Bagger Vance with Will [Smith] and Charlize [Theron], and that movie didn’t do well. And Will was, as he is now, the biggest star. And so it’s like, it’s not Will’s fault. [Laughs]

While The Legend of Bagger Vance may have had one of the best golf scenes in Hollywood history, it was definitely a box office bomb, grossing $39.5 million globally against a reported production budget of $80 million. Not to mention, the sports-drama film has low critics' score of 43% on Rotten Tomatoes. In the long run, it didn't hurt the careers of Damon, Smith or Theron, but I can understand why the Bourne star would've been shaken by the reception at that time.

Damon, unfortunately, experienced another setback after the release of Bagger Vance. There's another failed movie of Damon's that he's still not over, and it was released in 2000 as well:

And then I did All the Pretty Horses with Billy Bob [Thornton], and that was a whole fraught experience. There were different ideas between the studio and between Billy Bob about what the movie should be, and so it ended up getting cut in a way that wasn’t to Billy’s liking and it didn’t do well. And so I had had these misses. And so there was this stretch where the phone just didn’t ring. The silence was…. It was a real rose-colored lenses coming off.

I can imagine how frustrating that must have been to envision what you wanted your movie to be, only for the studio to take over. With that, it's hard not to wonder what could have been if Billy Bob Thornton had had his way. Ultimately, All the Pretty Horses was another bomb for Damon, as it made only $18.1 million worldwide on a budget of $57 million. As for its critics score on Rotten Tomatoes, it's at 33%, as of this writing.

Considering the Saving Private Ryan star's immense success, it's now somewhat wild to think about Damon worrying about his acting career, but it happens. He'd later experience a huge lull with no job offers, until Steven Soderbergh approached him about The Informant! The Ocean’s alum was so happy that he even offered to write the screenplay. While Scott Z. Burns ended up with the screenwriter role, Damon was still honored to be offered this leading role after a long career stretch.

It's so refreshing that Matt Damon has no problem looking back on the rougher points of his career. It’s also not unheard of for actors to look down on their own movies, but Damon speaks more diplomatically about Bagger Vance and All the Pretty Horses. I can imagine setbacks being hard to think about, but I get the sense that they've served as fuel for his career. And just look at him now. He's the lead of one of the biggest movies of all time and could even land himself some awards over the next few months.

On that note, The Odyssey is now available now available to rent on various digital platforms.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3572. LACMA Art+Film Gala: Nicole Kidman, Timothée Chalamet honor Denis Villeneuve

“It’s a pleasure to be here. You guys are just crazy party people,” said artist Vija Celmins as she summed up the jovial atmosphere at the 15th annual LACMA Art+Film Gala during her casual and off-the-cuff acceptance speech as one of the two honorees that night.

The annual fundraiser is a party, and unique among the many galas that hit the town this time of year. Along with raising money for the museum’s initiative to make film more central to its programming (this year it raised a record-breaking almost $7 million), it brings out an eclectic mix of A-list talent, up-and-coming filmmakers, and giants of the art world.

Honoree, Denis Villeneuve, Honoree Vija Celmins, co-chair Eva Chow and LACMA CEO Michael Govan

Just a quick scan of the packed room: Al Pacino sitting with artist Ed Ruscha and art dealer Larry Gagosian; artist Alex Israel wrapping his arm around Orlando Bloom for a photo; model Alex Consani crouching down to chat with influencer and comedian Quenlin Blackwell; and artists Jonas Wood and Mickalene Thomas chatting in one corner while Sarah Paulson and Parker Posey catch up in another.

Anya Taylor-Joy set the mood for the evening as one of the first arrivals on the red carpet, where talent posed in front of Chris Burden’s famed public art installation Urban Light. There in support of Dune director Denis Villeneuve, who was honored along with Celmins, the Dune: Part Two star wore a vintage 1997 Pierre Cardin haute couture bridal gown with a sheer silver overlay that looked both of the past and of the future.

Villeneuve's leading man, Timothée Chalamet, skipped the carpet all together, instead slipping into the crowded tent for dinner in a seat next to Villeneuve and his wife, producer Tanya Lapointe. Chalamet arrived separately from girlfriend Kylie Jenner, who did walk the carpet in a low-back Ashi Studio gown. When Jenner arrived at her table, she was seated opposite Chalamet, reaching across to grab his hand.

Seated next to Villeneuve was Nicole Kidman (in a voluminous, ballerina-inspired Chanel dress), who flew 15 hours from Australia to give Villeneuve his award. “The truth is I've never really met Denis. I've met him on some red carpets and sort of waved at him,” she said during her remarks. “Yet somehow I feel like I know the deepest parts of him because that is what extraordinary filmmakers do. They let you in. They reveal themselves to us through their work. They invite you into their imaginations, into their dreams, into their questions and into their fears.”

Monica Barbaro, Salma Hayek and Kim Kardashian

Before Villeneuve took the stage, a video capturing his film legacy of big, bold, and personal epics like Sicario, Blade Runner 2049, Arrival, and the Dune trilogy was played, featuring a slew of A-list directors singing his praises, including Steven Spielberg, Alfonso Cuaron, Alejandro G. Iñárritu, James Cameron, and Chloé Zhao. “I've always felt that cinema is seen as a pop art—the film carries the burden of being popular in the present,” said Villeneuve in his acceptance speech. “But at the end of the day, the real challenge is to make something that can enter the test of time.”

Speaking of tests (screen tests, that is) Villeneuve got a bit playful with the end of his speech, announcing to the room that he would right here, right now, announce which actor would play James Bond. The French-Canadian director is helming the next Bond film and over the past week, reports have been flying about who might be cast. Would Villeneuve put us all out of our misery and spill the beans? “The actor who will play the next James Bond is—and I will stop right now because [producer] Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack,” he said with a smile.

The gala, once again presented by Gucci, hosted a slew of this Oscar season’s most exciting young filmmakers, including Obsession filmmaker Curry Barker and Club Kid’s Jordan Firstman, along with La Bola Negra directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (known as Los Javis). The latter told me they didn’t plan to party as hard as they did at the Academy Museum Gala a few weeks ago, where they went viral for singing along to Taylor Swift's performance of "Love Story." Said Ambrossi, “I’m drinking only water tonight.”

Among the other guests, Joel Edgerton chatted with Abbott Elementary’s Quinta Brunson and Daniel Scheinert, one half of the Oscar-winning directing team Daniels (Everything Everywhere All at Once). Kim Kardashian wove her way through the crowd, pausing perfectly to look over her shoulder for a trailing photographer. And several stars made a date night out of the event: Sienna Miller brought fiancé Oli Green; Julia Garner sat with musician Charlie Walker; Viola Davis enjoyed the night with husband and producing partner Julius Tennon. Paris Hilton, who introduced Rosé onstage with her classic catchphrase “that’s hot,” wore a glittering Jenny Packham gown as she cascaded through the room with her husband Carter Reum.

Eva Chow, who had co-chaired the gala for the past 15 years with Leonardo DiCaprio, announced that she’d be stepping down from her post after this year. Dubbed the "Culture Queen of Los Angeles," she is credited with bringing together Hollywood and the art world for the event, helping grow it into the must-attend party of the season. DiCaprio couldn’t make it this year because he has a cold, but his girlfriend, model Vittoria Ceretti, was there to represent him.

But with all these big Hollywood types in the room, it was Celmins who stole the show—though she didn’t mean to. In a video that ran before her acceptance speech, the artist welcomed the video crew into her home, revealing her quick-witted humor, her ornery cat (she claims to be a dog person), and her love of Bob Dylan. Celmins is best known for her boundless work inspired by nature, including ocean waves, desert floors, starry night skies. She charmed the crowd with her boundless personality as well.

LACMA had plenty to celebrate this year, too. After a 20-year-long planning and development process, the David Geffen Galleries were completed this past year. As partygoers entered the tent for dinner, the silhouette of the formidable new building stood out in the background. “Same tent. Different buildings around it,” joked LACMA CEO Michael Govan during his opening remarks.

After his speech, Villeneuve and all the guests made their way out to LACMA’s main courtyard, where Rosé would perform under the stars. I joked with him that I thought he would make some news with that tease of a Bond casting, and then wondered if he likes being the center of attention at a gala like this. He said he values the connections he makes with other filmmakers and artists at these events. “I like talking one-on-one,” he said.

Noor Alfallah, Al Pacino, Erica Pelosini, Larry Gagosian and Ed Ruscha

While Rosé performed four songs for the black-tie-clad audience, Emily in Paris star Ashley Park and In the Heights actor Anthony Ramos swayed to her ballad, “Number One Girl.” Popcorn and cotton candy were passed out to the audience, who, naturally, sang along when Rosé ended her set with her biggest hit, “APT.” Andrew Garfield led his Artificial co-star Monica Barbaro by the hand through the crowd. Though the pair didn’t pose for photos on the carpet together, the couple (who have been romantically linked since 2025) spent the evening in close contact as they chatted with friends like Salma Hayek Pinault.

Villeneuve's speech best captured the evening’s one-of-a-kind mashup of art and film when he spoke passionately about the importance of human effort in the era of AI. “I can create something with a prompt or I can go into the desert with actors, with a crew and go on a real adventure where I learn about life and become better at my craft,” he said. “More important than the result is the process. The process is how the human experience acquires its meaning. In this moment in time, it is more important than ever that human beings keep making art together.”

#3571. The Bose Premium Smart Ultra Soundbar Is Now Cheaper Than It Was During Prime Day

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3570. This X-Men-Esque '80s Sci-Fi Series Launched Courteney Cox's Career

The premise of James D. Parriott's 1985 superhero/comedy series "Misfits of Science," which featured a young Courteney Cox, will sound very familiar to fans of Marvel Comics' X-Men titles.

The series follows a human scientist named Dr. Billy Hayes (Dean Paul Martin), who has taken an interest in what he called "human anomalies," which are people who have been born with a variety of unpredictable superpowers. In the show's pilot episode, he assembles the main cast of powerful castoffs with the intention of studying them, but also helping them come to terms with their supernatural abilities.

The team was small but mighty. It included Dr. Hayes' lab partner, Dr. Lincoln (Kevin Peter Hall), who can shrink for a limited period. Additionally, Mark Thomas Miller plays "Johnny B" Bukowski, a rocker who can suck up electricity and who wears shades to cover his glowing eyes. He can throw lightning bolts.

Most strikingly, Courteney Cox, future star of "Friends" and "Scream," plays Gloria, a troubled teen with "Carrie"-like telekinetic powers. "Misfits of Science" wasn't Cox's first credit: She had appeared in an episode of "As the World Turns" back in 1975, when she was still a kid, and famously danced with Bruce Springsteen in the "Dancing in the Dark" music video in 1984. "Misfits of Science," though, was the first time Cox starred in a TV series.

"Misfits of Science" is not currently available to stream, but resourceful media hunters will be able to find episodes online easily enough. It's a whimsical, lighthearted show that prodded at the conventions of superheroes as much as it vaunted them. It's definitely worth a glance.

"Misfits of Science," it should be noted, only lasted for a single 16-episode season, so it's okay if you don't remember it.

The series does have something of a superhero legacy, as R. Timothy Kring, a.k.a. Tim Kring, wrote an episode of "Misfits of Science," and he would go on to create the hit series "Heroes," the first season of which remains a must-watch (the later seasons, though, less so). Kring's "Misfits" episode, called "Twin Engines," is about a young man (Joel Polis) who is plagued with uncontrollable visions. It's eventually revealed that he was sharing the visions of his long-lost twin brother.

Indeed, the entire show was based on a long series of super-powered shenanigans and investigations. Mostly, the protagonists get involved in run-of-the-mill spy plots. The main characters aren't costumed vigilantes, but they do seem to operate as freelance spies. Famed drummer Mikey Jones appears in the show's pilot as a character with freezing powers named Ice Man. According to Giant Freakin' Robot, that character was abandoned after Marvel Comics "raised objections" over its own Ice Man character. And speaking of Marvel, Courteney Cox's character was very similar to the X-Men's Jean Gray.

Some fun trivia: Shortly after the time "Misfits of Science" was being made, Dr. Lincoln actor Kevin Peter Hall (who played the original Predator in John McTiernan's sci-fi action classic) was in contention to play either Data or Geordi La Forge on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." /Film has previously talked about all the finalists for the roles, and Hall eventually lost the roles to Brent Spiner and LeVar Burton, respectively.

As mentioned, "Misfits of Science" was not successful. Thanks to low ratings, the series was canceled before all of its episodes could even air, leaving one of them unaired in the United States.

Courteney Cox continued to work undeterred, of course. In 1987, she appeared in the low-budget, high-profile Cannon adaptation of "Masters of the Universe," a movie so goofy, it has been subjected to a "How Did This Get Made" oral history. That same year, she began playing the recurring role of Lauren Miller on the hit sitcom "Family Ties." By 1994, she was appearing in the comedy "Ace Ventura: Pet Detective" and began playing one of the six lead roles on "Friends." "Misfits of Science" was her first starring role, but it certainly wasn't her last.

You Can See Everything is the most talked-about movie on the 2026 movie schedule, and for good reason. There are many WTF moments that people have latched on to. There is one, it seems, that was left on the cutting room floor that Billy Evans just told the world about via X. It turns out, according to Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’ partner, got into a wrestling match with co-director Nathan Fielder. As wild as the movie got, this was not something I expected would happen, nor would I have expected it not to make the final cut.

Fielder is known for doing a lot of, let’s say, unconventional stuff in his projects, and that certainly holds true in You Can See Everything. Evans, for his part, seems to have been all in on going for it, too. There’s that now-infamous scene of Evans in the shower, a scene that he claims wasn’t his idea, disputing the claims of co-director Lance Oppenheim. Then there is this scene, as described by Evans on X:

I really wish they'd kept the scene where I wrestled Nathan, Borat style. Full top mount. His little Canadian frame struggling beneath me. I thought he was in on the joke. Until he wasn't. Imagine realizing that in camera.

Not only that, but according to Evans, Fielder ended up in the pool at the rented beach house where Evans and Holmes lived in the weeks leading up to Holmes’ imprisonment on fraud convictions and where most scenes with Evans and Holmes were filmed. Evans explains in a follow-up tweet after being asked if the two of them were naked:

Clothed. But Lance Oppenheim asked him to: 1) stand by the edge of the pool 2) remove his phone and monitor 3) look up Then I tossed Nathan into the pool. Borat wrestling ensued. I thought it was a bit. It wasn't.

He doesn’t go further into how it wasn’t a bit, or that Fielder was surprised by it. Honestly, knowing Fielder, I’d be pretty surprised myself if Fielder wasn’t in on it with Oppenheim. I guess anything is possible.

Evans also teased that there is a lot more that didn’t make the movie, saying in another tweet:

This literally wouldn't make the top 10 best deleted scenes. We didn't hold back. We showed them everything. You saw what they wanted to show you.... It was a wild experience. Hate us, [love] us, the truth or lack thereof is in the edit.

It’s hard to imagine that a director’s cut with added scenes could be better than the theatrical cut that we’ve all seen now, but if Fielder and Evans wrestling isn’t one of the top 10 best scenes left out, then I really hope the home release of You Can See Everything includes a lot more! Meanwhile, the film is closing in on a $100 million haul at the domestic box office, and that is just as astonishing as anything left out of the movie.

#3568. Fortnite Officially Reveals Pirate Shop Access Token Odds

How much are you willing to grind for each treasure?

Since Fortnite Treasure Hunters began on Nov. 1, Epic Games has been flooded with disgruntled fans wanting to know the odds of treasures that can be found in chests this season, namely the Pirate Shop Access token. Epic has finally relented, revealing the odds for each item and how much Treasure Hours influence them.

This season, the Pirate Shop Access token was introduced in Fortnite. The token is an item that, upon activation, makes every item sold in the Item Shop with in-game currency free for two weeks. It can be used twice: once in 2026 and again in 2027. This item has created an unpredictable frenzy among the community. Even though it's against Epic Games' terms of service, players have been selling accounts and offering token-hunting services at hourly rates.

The Pirate Shop Access token led fans to focus on opening chests rather than enjoying the highly-anticipated One Piece-themed season. After opening thousands of chests with no luck, fans wanted to know their chances of finding it. On Saturday, before Treasure Hours began, they spammed the hashtag ReleaseTheOdds, demanding Epic Games share the odds of each treasure in Fortnite. It finally complied.

According to Epic Games, the Pirate Shop Access token has a drop chance of 1 per 137,500 chests, which is the equivalent of 0.000007273%. Odds have not been tweaked throughout the season except for Treasure Hours timed-event — they were boosted 1.5x for the first Treasure Hour on Saturday, and 2x the second time around. The golden skin, which will rotate each week, is the rarest treasure players can find by far (1 per 1,562,500 chests), but it's safe to say that the token is still more desirable because it's worth the equivalent of thousands of dollars.

It's good that Epic Games was finally transparent with fans, but one question remains. The Solid Gold A$AP Rocky outfit has now rotated out of the weekly treasures available, replaced by Solid Gold Lil Uzi Vert. These skins are free to find during Treasure Hunters, but it is unknown whether either will be available for purchase in the future. If not, they would become the rarest cosmetics in Fortnite history.

Nov. 14 marks the last set of Treasure Hours before the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6, so if you're still grinding for the token, this is the best time to try to find it. The season ends on Dec. 5, so gamers can still search for it on Nov. 21 and 28 if they're willing to put GTA 6 aside for a couple of hours.

#3567. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3565. This Chilling Japanese Folk Horror Series Is One Of Hulu's Best Hidden Gems

If you're in the mood for a discrete dose of folk horror, Hulu recently added Adam Scott's terrifying horror "Hokum." But if you'd like to extend your trauma over, say two seasons of sheer terror, then "Gannibal" is for you. The show stars Yuya Yagira as a police officer who leaves the city to start over in a remote village. Here, he quickly discovers things aren't quite as idyllic as they seem.

"Gannibal" premiered in December 2022 but has failed to make much of an impact outside of Japan, despite arguably being one of the best horror series of the 2020s. Thus far, two seasons of "Gannibal" have been released, and had they hit Netflix in the United States, the show may well have become a big hit stateside. As it stands, this is one of Japan's best kept secrets and it's waiting to be discovered on Hulu.

Masaaki Ninomiya's "Gannibal" manga was originally serialized across thirteen volumes from October 2018 to November 2021. In October of that year, it was announced that "Gannibal" would be adapted as a TV series, with Shinzo Katayama directing from teleplays by Takamasa Oe.Thankfully, it turned out to be a worthy adaptation.

One of the best foreign horror shows streaming right now, "Gannibal" shares much in common with the South Korean horror movie with a 99% Rotten Tomatoes score "The Wailing." Both are set in remote villages and follow a police officer who becomes increasingly menaced by some terrifying ancient evil. But "Gannibal" departs from the movie with its tale of a cannibal conspiracy.

Yuya Yagira plays police officer Daigo Agawa, who after an unfortunate ordeal in Tokyo moves to the small mountain village of Kuge with his wife Yuki Agawa (Riho Yoshioka) and daughter Mashiro Agawa (Kokone Shimizu). At first, this secluded hamlet seems like the ideal refuge from the city and Agawa's fraught past. But things get off to an eerie start as Kuge's previous police officer has mysteriously vanished.

As Agawa and his family become more acquainted with the village and its people they discover the Goto family essentially run the town, and they don't seem like the most charming bunch. Meanwhile, a woman's body is found on the mountain, and while the Gotos claim she was killed by a bear, Agawa notices a human bite mark. Soon, his family's escape starts to turn into a nightmare. As such, this is not a horror TV show you can watch with the whole family. But it definitely deserves your attention regardless.

While you may never have heard of "Gannibal," the series has become a sensation in its native Japan. In April 2025, The Hollywood Reporter reported that "Gannibal" had become the most-viewed title in the country on Disney+ since its second season debuted in March of that year. The show also set new records for the streamer, solidifying its status as a bonafide mega-hit in Japan. In the United States, however, "Gannibal" mostly flew under the radar.

There are no "top critic" reviews for the series on Rotten Tomatoes, and it hasn't shown up on any "best horror series" lists since its 2022 debut. But it has managed to generate a small amount of buzz among non-Japanese viewers. One Redditor described the series as "grim folk horror" and was evidently left "completely wrecked" by it. Elsewhere on Reddit, another user described the series as "like 'Midsommar' meets 'Resident Evil 7'" and praised the "amazing actors, great cinematography, chilling and memorable soundtrack, and an absurdly dark story."

Letterboxd users are similarly impressed. "I just love it," writes one, who goes on to commend the series for its "sharp plot," "creepy characters," and "unsettling vibes," as well as the "splendid cinematography." Another also highlighted how the show is "beautifully shot and incredibly well-acted." Unfortunately, it seems unlikely there will be more to come. "Gannibal" Season 2 was released on March 19, 2025 and that wrapped up the story told in Masaaki Ninomiya's manga. Thankfully, if you are able to binge your way through both seasons of the series, there are plenty of great folk horror movies to tide you over.

#3563. Patrick Stewart's '90s Fantasy Movie With Neve Campbell Is Streaming For Free

An adaptation of Oscar Wilde's 1887 short story, Sydney Macartney's "The Canterville Ghost" aired on ABC on January 27, 1996, and, perhaps surprisingly, featured notable central roles for both the late legend Sir Patrick Stewart and Neve Campbell. Indeed, 1996 was a banner year for both actors, with Stewart appearing in the film "Star Trek: First Contact" and Campbell headlining two of the best teen movies of the 1990s over the same 12-month period (namely, "The Craft" and "Scream"). Stewart, of course, was already riding high professionally by that point. But for Campbell, this was the final vault before proper stardom following her breakout role on the hit series "Party of Five."

It should be noted that Wilde's original story is a light tale about a haunted mansion, and Macartney's TV movie — which is currently streaming for free on platforms like Tubi and Prime Video — affects a similarly lighthearted tone. Wilde's source material concerns the Otises, a family of two parents and three children who move into Canterville Castle, despite warnings that it is haunted. Sure enough, its ghost tries to frighten them off, but the Otises react with mere annoyance. For example, when Mrs. Otis spots a bloodstain on the carpet, she dryly states, "I don't at all care for blood-stains in a sitting-room."

Macartney's adaptation transposes the action to the modern day. In the movie, the Otises inevitably have to deal with the specter of Sir Simon de Canterville, played by Stewart. Campbell, meanwhile, plays the young Virginia Otis, and the story is told largely from her perspective. As for Sir Simon, he eventually reveals the trauma that left him in his ghostly state, which has to do with his beloved dead wife, Eleanor.

The TV movie version of "The Canterville Ghost" adds a few fun flourishes to the story. The Otis family patriarch, Hiram, is played by Edward Wiley, and there comes a scene where Virginia and the Ghost, having begun communicating, have to convince Hiram that ghosts are real. In a nod to Sir Patrick Stewart's past with the Royal Shakespeare Company, Virginia and the Ghost get Hiram's attention by staging a scene from "Hamlet" wherein Sir Simon plays the Ghost of Hamlet's Father. Fittingly enough, Stewart would later portray both the Ghost of Hamlet's Father and Claudius in a celebrated 2008 BBC production of the play opposite David Tennant.

Initially, as mentioned, Sir Simon is determined to scare away the Otis family to remain in his sad, ghostly state. Soon after moving in, however, Virginia finds a secret passageway inside the Canterville Castle leading to a chamber where Sir Simon hangs out during the daylight hours. Soon, she and her brothers befriend Sir Simon, and we learn that, despite his intense demeanor, he isn't so terrible or scary. (Virginia's brothers even startle Sir Simon with a fake ghost puppet they construct themselves.) At the same time, Virginia develops a crush on Francis, the Duke of Cheshire (Daniel Betts), a local nobleman who plays a larger role here than he does in Oscar Wilde's original story.

The central drama arises when Hiram believes Virginia is responsible for Sir Simon's shenanigans and threatens to send her back home to the U.S., where she won't be able to flirt with Francis anymore. This is basically her motivation for proving the ghost is real because, again, "The Canterville Ghost" is a fairly fanciful yarn.

There aren't a lot of professional reviews of the "Canterville Ghost" TV movie readily available. One can find a write-up on Common Sense Media by Brian Costello, who gave the film a high rating (which indicates that it's perfectly okay for younger kids). Costello also praised Patrick Stewart, writing that he brings a Shakespearean relish to his character. "[H]is performance," the review reads, "more than makes up for the dated special effects."

David Saunderson, writing for the British/Irish horror website Spooky Isles, had some mild complaints about how the TV movie strays from Oscar Wilde's original story. With weary resignation, he observed that Otises had to be made American for American audiences, despite being British in Wilde's source material. He added that the movie isn't as good as the 1944 film adaptation starring Charles Laughton in the title role and that he found the modern contrivances to be a little tiresome, despite Stewart's solid work. As he put it:

"Patrick Stewart is a fine actor, and fine actors make fine Canterville Ghosts — he's very dramatic, a bit scary, and works well with Neve Campbell [...] who plays the Otis daughter who hates that she has been brought to England but soon befriends the ghost and learns from the experience — blah, blah, blah — usual teenage angst in TV movie!"

Notably, 1996's "The Canterville Ghost" won an Emmy for Outstanding Individual Achievement in Music Composition for a Miniseries or Special, which is no small feat. Stream it now, and see what you make of it.

#3562. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3561. WoW: Forever Boosts Dungeon XP As Blizzard Struggles to Get Leveling Balance Right

Dungeons were heavily nerfed during beta; now they're back, sort of

Blizzard just gave some ground in its battle to get players to slow down and spend more time in the open world in World of Warcraft: Forever.

The developer applied a hotfix on Sunday that boosted experience points (XP) for killing monsters in dungeons by 50%. It's Blizzard's first concession to complaints from players that dungeons, a core part of the WoW experience, had become too unrewarding to play compared to questing in the open world.

Blizzard is struggling to find the sweet spot for leveling in WoW: Forever. The intention is that leveling in Forever should be faster and smoother than it was in classic WoW (which is definitely the case), but that the journey to level 60 should still feel substantial. Additionally, Blizzard is keen to promote the open-world questing experience and avoid players spending all their time running dungeons just to race to the finish line.

When the beta began, XP from killing monsters in dungeons was heavily reduced compared to WoW Classic, while XP for completing dungeon quests was dramatically increased — the idea being that dungeons would be worth running once, but after that, you'd return to questing.

Whether you're a newbie, a returning player, or a devotee of modern WoW, you should bear these things in mind

Then, in an attempt to slow down leveling that was generally perceived to be too fast, Blizzard nerfed dungeon quest XP too, partway through the beta. But many players felt this change trivialized dungeon runs to the extent that they no longer wanted to do them at all. Hence this latest adjustment, presumably made after Blizzard noticed too few players in dungeons over the game's launch weekend.

Players have mostly reacted positively to the change while criticizing Blizzard for flip-flopping and making overcorrections. One thing's for sure, though — this latest boost to XP will only speed up leveling in WoW: Forever. And this comes after a group of five players became the first to hit level 60 on Friday after just 52 hours. It seems likely there'll be more changes yet to come.

Thank you for subscribing to our newsletter,

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

I think maybe bonus exp for the first time completing a dungeon, increased for each new member, then lowering it a bit afterwards, gives you a reason to be excited for new dungeons as well as reason to help new players through it.

The James Bond movies have been entertaining audiences for decades, with entire generations brought up on 007's adventures. Daniel Craig's Bond movies ended with No Time to Die, opening the door for a new actor to take on the mantle in the developing 26th movie by Denis Villeneuve. Fans have spent years taking bets on the next Bond, and the Oscar-nominated filmmaker recently trolled us at a recent event.

No Time to Die's ending shockingly killed off 007, a first for the long-running franchise (which is streaming with an Amazon Prime subscription). Those involved with the next movie have been keeping tight-lipped about casting, but Villeneuve spoke at the LACMA Art + Film Gala, where he spoke to the crowd and said:

With the blessing of my new friends at Amazon, I will reveal to you tonight who will be the next James Bond. The actor who will play the next James Bond is… And I will stop right now because Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack.

What a tease. Clearly the acclaimed director knows that folks are dying to know who will take on the role of 007 in his James Bond movie. And what's a little light trolling among friends? Hopefully we'll get more answers about his developing blockbuster once Dune: Part Three hits theaters this December as half of Dunesday.

Denis Villeneuve's involvement in Bond 26 helping to buoy excitement for the mysterious project... even if we still don't know who will be playing the lead role. In a video from Variety's Instagram, he got honest about why he can't say much right now, offering:

I should not comment right now because every word I’m going to say is going to be scrutinized. I would just say that I’m having a great time.

The Arrival director was being cheeky at the event, but these comments show a much more sincere side of him. He's clearly thrilled to be behind the camera for the next James Bond movie, even if fans are desperate for any information regarding casting. You can see a video of him giving the above quote below:

It's been years since No Time to Die hit theaters back in 2021, fans have been curious about which actor will be passed the baton from Daniel Craig. Unfortunately we're still waiting on casting news, with fans tossing around a number of familiar names online. There are tons of rumors about who might be playing the martini-sipping agent, as well as chatter that the studio might go with an unknown rather than an established actor. Hopefully we get some answers soon.

All of the Bond movies are streaming on Amazon, and Denis Villeneuve's Dune: Part Three hits theaters December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. Fingers crossed that more Bond 26 info comes after that title gets its wide theatrical release.

#3559. Benito Skinner’s ‘Overcompensating’ Returns for Season 2: More Laughs, More Sex, More Gay

It’s been a year and a half since the first season of Benito Skinner’s Prime Video comedy series, Overcompensating, debuted, and a lot has changed for him in that time. For one, Skinner—also known as Benny Drama, his online alter ego—is blond now. It’s a change he says may be permanent or perhaps semipermanent. “It’s how I see myself—as a blond,” he tells me over Zoom. “So we’re going to keep going with it for a sec.”

But Skinner has transformed in much less superficial ways since the launch of his hit Amazon series, which is based on his experiences coming out as gay as a Georgetown undergrad. Equal parts raunchy and heartwarming, the first season follows Benny (Skinner), a closeted former high school football player who attempts to navigate the chaos of college, where he forms an unlikely bond with a fellow student named Carmen (Wally Baram).

Skinner shares that making the second installment of the series was “way more fluid, way less stressed.” As it should have been. The first season was a popular hit for the streamer (it has a 93% fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes), hard-launching Skinner as an exciting new voice plucked from the internet and ready for prime time.

Benny and Carmen begin the season as enemies.

The second season, which Vanity Fair can exclusively reveal will debut on February 17, 2027, expands the world he created with new storylines for the supporting characters—and bigger stakes for Benny as he comes into his own with his sexuality. Benny navigates not only coming out to his sister, Grace (Mary Beth Barone), and his parents (Connie Britton and Kyle MacLachlan), but also his own sexual exploration—and all the awkwardness that comes with it.

So much of what made the first season a hit—the awkward comedy, the silly themed parties, the talking Megan Fox poster—returns, but this time many of the characters grapple with deeper issues. Yet Skinner felt lighter making the show this time around. “I think in season one, Benny is that stressed, so that kind of worked,” he says. “But in this one, we’re having more fun. He has some joy, so we can loosen up a little bit.”

Connie Britton, center, reprises her role as Benny's mom.

After Overcompensating premiered, Skinner was approached, he says, by “a few gays” who told him, “I thought it’d be gayer, the show.” He promises that the second season delivers just that: “We’re creeping out of the closet,” says Skinner.

In the first season, Benny is trying to find his place on campus while constantly living in fear that the people around him will discover he’s gay. He falls for a dashing British classmate named Miles (Rish Shah), only to find out he is straight and has kissed Carmen. The season ends with Carmen revealing that she has also slept with Grace’s boyfriend, Peter (Adam DiMarco), and in the final moments, Carmen accidentally lets slip in front of Grace that Benny is gay.

Skinner and Lukas Gage reunite in season two.

In the upcoming season, Benny heads back home with his sister for the start of Christmas break, struggling because he hasn’t yet come out to his family. “If season one was about friends, I think this season is about family, and trying to reintroduce yourself to your parents after starting to become yourself,” says Skinner. The way his father finds out about it makes for an especially tense moment, and Benny goes to great lengths (like joining the crew team) to mend that bond with his dad. “That relationship between gay men and father, I think, is always fraught and confusing,” he says. “I just wanted to make it as honest as possible.”

At the start of the new season, Benny and Carmen are at odds; Grace and her boyfriend, Peter, have broken up; and many of the characters are exploring those feelings of loneliness that can crop up in college. A handful of exciting new faces also join this season. Australian actor Aisha Dee (The Bold Type) plays a new student who becomes an instant It girl on campus. AnnaSophia Robb (The Carrie Diaries) joins as an intense coxswain (the one who does the yelling) on the crew team. And Tony-nominated stage actor Tom Francis (Sunset Boulevard) plays the captain of the team, serving as Benny’s newest love interest.

Peter (Adam DiMarco) is looking for his path forward.

For Skinner, the second season is about capturing the ups and downs of coming out. It’s not just one reveal and then you’re out of the closet and everything is better. “I get to be even more specific about coming out and also tell a story that I think I haven’t seen yet done in this way, which is the complication of coming out—how you can take 10 steps forward, a hundred steps back,” he says.

Benny joins the crew team, where he meets a new love interest (Tom Francis).

There’s also a lot more sex. “There are a couple scenes that are definitely going to be off-limits for the family,” Skinner says. But of course, in Overcompensating, the sex scenes aren’t always smooth sailing. “I think our show is about trying to be sexy and then it going wrong, or feeling like you start to come into yourself but you get made a fool,” he says.

Skinner adds the title of executive music producer to his résumé this season. “It feels like a return to my radio-DJ roots, and that feels right,” he says. There’s more Britney Spears and Charli xcx (who appeared in a cameo last season), and he wanted the show’s music to remain an important part of the world. He even wrote a letter to Coldplay when he wanted to use the band’s song “Fix You” in this new season. “I love doing the letters to these guys because I’m like, So is Chris Martin reading this? Is this sent by owl? What’s the vibe?” he says with a smile.

Overcompensating’s return will come almost two years after its debut, and Skinner, who says he always plans to keep this story set in the characters’ college years, wants to make the wait a little shorter next time. “I apologize to everyone that it took a while,” he says. “TV takes a long time, so I’m trying to go faster, but daddy has to write it.”

“I don’t want any of these characters to feel like we’re pandering to maybe what we think the internet will want,” says Skinner of crafting the second installment after a hit first season.

“What I wanted to do is surprise people with where we took it,” says Skinner of the new season, “and have them be like, ‘Oh, this isn’t what I asked for, but it is something kind of delicious and new.’”

#3558. Patrick Dempsey's Thanksgiving Horror Movie Is Worth Revisiting This Holiday Season

Eli Roth's 2023 slasher flick "Thanksgiving" follows various citizens of Plymouth, Massachusetts, as they find themselves being targeted by a killer dressed as the famed Pilgrim John Carver in the lead-up to the titular holiday. Realizing that these murders are related to a Black Friday trampling incident from the previous year (which led to three people dying), it falls to Plymouth's sheriff, Eric Newlon (Patrick Dempsey), to figure out who's been taking some Turkey Day-related revenge.

There aren't too many scary flicks centered around this particular holiday, but Roth's film has now joined the modest pantheon of Thanksgiving horror movies that includes Brad F. Grinter's schlock classic "Blood Freak," the utterly absurd "ThanksKilling," the pointed anticapitalist flick "Black Friday," and Oliver Blackburn's "Kristy." Indeed, Roth's "Thanksgiving" is the perfect horror movie to watch this November, or any November, really. Like most of his other R-rated offerings, its gore is gleefully over the top, and there's gallows humor present throughout.

"Thanksgiving" began its life as a fake trailer that Roth directed for 2007's two-in-one "Grindhouse," itself an attempt by directors Robert Rodriguez and Quentin Tarantino to recreate the experience of going to a rundown grindhouse double feature circa the 1970s or '80s. They each helmed one down-and-dirty B-movie, giving them fake film scratches and print wear to boot. The program also featured a brief reel of previews for non-existent B-movies, one of which was the gory slasher "Thanksgiving." It took Roth 16 years, but he later expanded that fake promo into a real feature film. Now, it's appointment holiday viewing.

"Thanksgiving" was, by dint of its novelty, something of a hit. On a budget of only $15 million, it made $46.6 million at the box office and, perhaps surprisingly, earned pretty good reviews. Not only that, "Thanksgiving" also has a higher critical approval score on Rotten Tomatoes than any of Eli Roth's other feature-length directorial efforts, among them the mostly well-received "The House with a Clock in Its Walls" and the critically lambasted bomb "Borderlands."

"Thanksgiving" seemingly got a lot of mileage from its creative kills. One victim, for instance, is murdered, cooked, trussed up like a turkey, and served at a table surrounded by hostages and victims. (This kill is featured in Roth's original fake trailer as well.) In addition, "Thanksgiving" features the kind of fun, splattery deaths that slasher fans crave, among them a decapitation, a disemboweling, and a trampoline stabbing.

Meanwhile, Patrick Dempsey's character is crucial to the movie's central plot, which makes sense, seeing as the actor is the film's big celebrity "get." Pop singer Addison Rae, Nell Verlaque, Jalen Thomas Brooks (aka Mateo from "The Pitt"), and Milo Manheim round out the cast, with Gina Gershon joining them in a small role.

The Black Friday trampling might make one think that "Thanksgiving" is constructed as a pointed anti-shopping satire, lampooning the bizarreness that takes place at many retail outlets the day after Thanksgiving. Roth, however, is more keen on dark humor and gooey gore than anything thoughtful. That's more of his métier. However you feel about the filmmaker, he certainly knows the power of ridiculous kill scenes.

Again, critics generally accepted "Thanksgiving" as good, silly fun. Alonso Duralde and Christy Lemire, the co-hosts of the review show "Breakfast All Day," were both positive on the film, with Duralde saying that it makes for a great movie to see with a crowd and Lemire stressing that she had a great time. They both loved the film's cast, too, with Lemire admiring that, Addison Rae notwithstanding, it wasn't just famous person stunt casting. Eli Roth even commented on the movie's casting in an exclusive interview with /Film, so he is at least astute in that regard.

Reviewing "Thanksgiving" for IndieWire, Alison Foreman gave the film an A-, writing:

"With more time dedicated to table-setting than gorging on gore, Roth and [writer Jeff] Rendell create a living-breathing corner of the United States that's actually worth terrorizing. The people populating this fictional version of Plymouth don't feel 'real,' per se, but they're toxically relatable, and the complicated relationship they have with Thanksgiving is as politically charged as it is annoyingly pointless in life."

Foreman's only issue with "Thanksgiving" was that it relies very heavily on characters checking Instagram to tell its story, and it makes a lot of references to billionaire mogul Mark Cuban (!), meaning the film will feel incredibly dated very quickly. Although, she did enjoy the soundtrack, which includes bands like the Misfits and The Waitresses.

But then, all films become dated eventually, so that's hardly a cardinal sin. If you're looking for a fun Thanksgiving movie this holiday, and you are allergic to sentimentality, then maybe "Thanksgiving" will be more your beat.

#3557. This New Chrome AI Feature Reads Your Gmail to Make Filling Out Web Forms Easier

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3556. Deadpool 2's Rob Delaney Debunks Popular X-Men Fan Theory About His Character Peter

No, X-Men fans, Peter from "Deadpool 2" and "Deadpool & Wolverine" is not Peter Wisdom. Peter actor Rob Delaney confirmed this in a red carpet interview with ScreenRant, and we offer our deepest nerd condolences to anyone who may have been invested in this.

The presence of Delaney's character Peter, a supporting player in David Leitch's 2018 action/comedy "Deadpool 2," is a joke unto itself. Deadpool (Ryan Reynolds) is assembling a team of superheroes called the X-Force that he intends to employ for a skydiving-based rescue mission. Deadpool is such a non-credible deadbeat, though, that he can't afford to be too choosy about who joins his team. He recruits characters like Shatterstar (Lewis Tan), Domino (Zazie Beetz), and Bedlam (Terry Crews), but also deigns to take on Peter, a regular, kind of dorky middle-aged guy with no superpowers.

When the trailer for "Deadpool 2" first dropped, /Film theorized that Delaney could be playing Peter Wisdom, an X-Men character with deep ties to X-Force. The character was first introduced in an issue of the Britain-set X-Men comic "Excalibur," dated February of 1995, and, like all comic book characters, he underwent multiple dramatic life events in a very short amount of time. He dated Shadowcat, became the mentor for X-Force, seemingly died, returned, and became the head of a spy agency. In the comics, Pete Wisdom can absorb heat from the environment around him and channel it into magical "hot knives" that protrude from his fingers.

The character also starred in his own series of comics in 2006 called simply "Wisdom," and he likely has at least a few fans out there. For those who think he appeared in the "Deadpool" movies, though, that wasn't Peter Wisdom. That was just Peter.

The issue of Peter's identity may be a little confusing, as sources like Wikipedia list Rob Delaney as definitely playing Pete Wisdom in both "Deadpool 2" and the 2024 follow-up "Deadpool & Wolverine." On IMDb, however, his proper credit of just "Peter" is retained. In the red carpet interview, Delaney was 100% unambiguous on the matter, saying:

"Peter Wisdom is a guy from the comics. My character is not Peter Wisdom. He's just a guy named Peter. And I think maybe they arbitrarily gave him the last initial 'W,' which explains the confusion. But in fact, [he's] just Peter, created from whole cloth by the writers."

Sometimes actors in Marvel Comics-based movies have to be coy about spoilers and plot details, but it seems that Delaney is not being coy in this case. He seems to genuinely be saying he isn't playing Pete Wisdom.

The arc of Delaney's actual character is pretty hilarious unto itself. Peter is recruited into X-Force, meets a grisly fate, is saved through the miracle of time travel, and then proves to be deeply beloved across the multiverse in "Deadpool & Wolverine." Peter turns up in that film's climax, which involves hundreds of parallel-universe Deadpools pouring through an interdimensional portal to fight each other. When Peter arrives on the scene, however, every Deadpool pauses to marvel at his presence. It seems that all Deadpools have a Peter in their home dimension, and that they all hold him in very high esteem. The hundreds of Deadpools embrace Peter, and he enjoys the attention.

With a universe as long-lived and complex as Marvel Comics, of course, some fans may happily chime in with an optimistic "never say die" attitude about Rob Delaney playing Pete Wisdom. Indeed, as "Deadpool & Wolverine" proved, every character in the Marvel Cinematic Universe has an untold number of parallel doppelgängers from all across the multiverse. Even if the original Pete Wisdom is a suave British James Bond-type with heat knife powers, and the movie Peter is a dippy American everyman, there's no reason why those characters can't be one and the same across the multiverse, right?

And, heck, "Deadpool 2" made a lot of vital changes to known comic book characters, including the aforementioned Shatterstar, a.k.a Rusty. In the comics, Shatterstar is an interdimensional traveler from Mojoworld, something he does explain in "Deadpool 2." But in the movie, he doesn't become a vital member of the team. Indeed, he has an unfortunate run-in with a helicopter. Deadpool, thereafter, quips that no one is going to miss Shatterstar. Nonetheless, the character returned for a very brief cameo in "Deadpool & Wolverine."

So why not do something like that for Pete Wisdom? As of this writing, /Film has been gathering information about the upcoming X-Men film from Marvel Studios, citing a familiar line-up and keeping track of pieces of casting. (Inde Navarrette from "Obsession" has been cast as the character of Rogue, for instance.) Time will tell if the makers of the new X-Men will have enough of a sense of humor to cast Rob Delaney as Pete Wisdom.

#3555. Mass Effect Creator Is ‘Optimistic’ the Series Will Live On

Fans and developers remain confident that Mass Effect will return

BioWare's shutdown has been one of the hardest studio closures in gaming history. The Edmonton-based studio made its way into thousands of gamers' hearts, and it was set to continue this mission with the development of Mass Effect Universe, the next entry in the Mass Effect series. The project may have been canceled, but hope still lingers.

In 2020, in celebration of N7 Day, the annual celebration of the Mass Effect franchise, BioWare announced that it was working on a new Mass Effect game, but it was only in the early stages of development. Besides a handful of teasers, not much was heard about the project from then on. When private investors bought EA, Mass Effect 5 seemed increasingly unlikely. Unfortunately, that proved true: EA shut down BioWare and canceled the project on Oct. 21, 2026, nearly six years after its announcement.

However, neither fans nor developers were ready to give up on Mass Effect just yet. Petitions were created, billboards were put up to raise awareness, voice actors showed support, and developers even leaked an early trailer to fuel the fire. The community has come together, celebrating N7 Day in a uniquely special way.

Casey Hudson, project director for the Mass Effect trilogy, also spoke up on N7 Day. He showed confidence in the series' future and thanked fans for continuing to make N7 Day a special occasion. Hudson underlined that "when Mass Effect makes its triumphant return, it will be thanks to the outpouring of love from players around the world." The message was particularly special coming from one of the series creators. While Casey's words shouldn't be taken as an official statement nor a promise, as the series' IP remains firmly in EA's hands, it was a boost of morale that gave fans another dose of much-needed hope.

Commander Shepard's voice actors, Mark Meer and Jennifer Hale, have also shown immense support for this cause, alongside other cast members. The two have made videos on social media promoting the petition in hopes that another company will pick up the project, rescuing it from the graveyard of IPs affected by EA's studio closures. It has been weeks since the project was canceled, but the community remains hopeful that this is not the end of Mass Effect. Only time will tell.
