#3554. 10 '90s Teen Movies That Remain Essential Viewing Today

Teenagers had it rough in the '90s. You could destroy your social life before lunch, and there was no group chat to warn you it was happening. On the plus side, you could disappear into a shopping mall for six hours without anybody tracking your location.

The movies were pretty spectacular, though, as was the music of the '90s. Hollywood gave teenagers their own stories and, occasionally, allowed them to behave like actual teenagers. They could be obnoxious, selfish, or catastrophically stupid without the screenplay rushing to teach them a valuable lesson. And while Clueless made adolescence look fabulous, filmmakers such as John Singleton were telling very different stories about what it meant to grow up in America.

The best '90s teen movies remain surprisingly easy to relate to, even for an audience that has never used a pay phone. Others, including the controversial Kids, offer an unsettling look at teenage life that feels almost too authentic. These 10 classics capture a generation that was figuring things out largely without supervision, and sometimes paying a terrible price for it.

Cher Horowitz has opinions about everything, and most of them are wrong. That's what makes her such excellent company. Amy Heckerling's inspired update of Jane Austen's Emma follows a Beverly Hills teenager who attempts to organize everyone else's happiness with the confidence of someone who has never seriously considered the consequences. Alicia Silverstone is hilarious as Cher, whose carefully curated world begins unraveling when she discovers that other people have feelings, too.

The jokes are still quick, and the fashion remains fabulous, but Clueless is smarter than its heroine initially appears. Cher genuinely wants to help people, yet she can barely imagine that anyone might want something different from what she has planned. Her journey toward self-awareness is surprisingly relatable, especially for teenagers navigating the exhausting social politics of high school. Plus, there's something refreshing about a movie that allows a girl to love fashion without treating her as an idiot.

It's the last day of school in 1976, and Richard Linklater has no intention of inventing a complicated plot simply because Hollywood expects one. Instead, Dazed and Confused follows a sprawling group of Texas teenagers through an increasingly eventful night. The freshmen are trying to avoid humiliation, the older kids are partying, and Matthew McConaughey's Wooderson is still hanging around high school long after he should have moved on. Everybody knows somebody like Wooderson. Unfortunately.

Despite being set in the '70s, this is one of the quintessential '90s films, arriving with a cast that included future stars Ben Affleck and Parker Posey. The classic rock soundtrack is phenomenal, but Linklater's real achievement is his understanding of teenage social dynamics. Nobody wants to be the person who ruins the night, even when things are clearly getting out of hand. Dazed and Confused also makes absolutely no apologies for letting its characters waste time. After all, isn't that half the point of being young?

The shopping mall was practically a second home for teenagers in the 1990s, which makes Kevin Smith's Mallrats something of a historical document. Jason Lee and Jeremy London star as Brodie and T.S., two recently dumped young men who retreat to the mall to complain about their relationships and generally accomplish nothing. Naturally, Jay and Silent Bob are also hanging around, ensuring that the afternoon becomes far more ridiculous than anyone intended.

Technically, the central characters are a little beyond their teenage years, although their behavior suggests otherwise. Smith's irreverent dialogue and affection for comic books helped make Mallrats a cult favorite despite its disappointing theatrical release. There's a certain beauty to how completely unproductive its characters are, particularly in a world where young people now seem expected to turn every hobby into a business. Sometimes a trip to the mall was simply a trip to the mall, and you might even run into Stan Lee.

There was a time when working at a record store was a legitimate aspiration, particularly if you wanted to spend your days surrounded by music and people who understood your questionable taste in bands. Empire Records takes place at an independent music shop whose employees discover that their beloved workplace could become another corporate chain. Their attempts to save it are spectacularly disorganized, but they're also enormously entertaining.

Liv Tyler and Renée Zellweger lead a young ensemble cast navigating personal problems while preparing for an appearance by the magnificently unbearable Rex Manning. The film was a commercial disappointment, but its reputation grew considerably through home video and an enduring cult following. More importantly, Empire Records captures a specific moment when musical taste could feel like your entire identity. The soundtrack alone deserves attention, and anyone who has ever worked in retail will appreciate just how badly this particular day goes off the rails. Damn the man. Save the Empire.

Kat Stratford would probably hate being described as relatable. Too bad. Julia Stiles makes the fiercely independent teenager one of the most memorable romantic comedy heroines of the decade, while Heath Ledger brings an irresistible swagger to Patrick Verona. Their relationship begins under decidedly dishonest circumstances: Patrick has been paid to date Kat so that her younger sister can pursue a boy of her own.

Inspired by Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, the movie has enough sense to question some of its source material's assumptions about women. Kat doesn't need to become more agreeable to deserve affection, and Patrick ultimately has to confront his own dishonesty. The supporting cast is equally entertaining, particularly Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Larisa Oleynik as the film's other romantic pairing. Ledger's famous bleacher serenade remains glorious, although Stiles' delivery of the title poem is the moment that gives this comedy its emotional punch.

Long before Hollywood became obsessed with cinematic universes, Kid 'n Play were just trying to get to a party. Reginald Hudlin's House Party follows high school student Kid, played by Christopher Reid, who sneaks out after being grounded to attend a gathering hosted by his best friend Play, played by Christopher Martin. Getting there proves complicated, especially with a trio of school bullies determined to make Kid's life miserable.

The movie is an irresistible snapshot of early-'90s hip-hop culture, with a soundtrack that practically demands an impromptu dance battle. There's plenty of outrageous comedy, but the central friendship gives the film its appeal, while Robin Harris is hilarious as Kid's perpetually exasperated father. House Party also offered young Black audiences a mainstream comedy that celebrated their culture without making crime or tragedy the central attraction. The famous dance-off remains one of the great musical moments in teen cinema, and the film's infectious energy hasn't diminished.

Shakespeare probably never imagined his famous tragedy unfolding amid Hawaiian shirts and speeding cars, but Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet makes a convincing argument that he might have approved. Leonardo DiCaprio and Claire Danes play the doomed lovers, whose families remain locked in a bitter feud in modern-day Verona Beach. The original dialogue survives, although the swords have become guns and the Montagues look suspiciously like members of a boy band.

Luhrmann understands that teenagers don't experience first love in moderation. Every stolen glance feels monumental, and every disagreement threatens the end of civilization. The film's extravagant visual style perfectly suits that emotional intensity, particularly during Romeo and Juliet's first encounter through an aquarium. Its soundtrack also introduced a generation to an eclectic collection of artists, including Radiohead and Garbage. Anyone who thinks Shakespeare is inherently boring should be required to watch this before making that argument again.

John Singleton was just 23 when he directed Boyz n the Hood, which remains one of the most extraordinary debuts in American cinema. Set in South Central Los Angeles, the film follows Tre Styles, played by Cuba Gooding Jr., and his childhood friends as they approach adulthood in a neighborhood shaped by gang violence and deeply entrenched inequality. Laurence Fishburne is unforgettable as Tre's father, Furious, whose determination to prepare his son for the realities of the world gives the movie some of its most powerful scenes.

There's a temptation to treat Boyz n the Hood as an entirely different kind of teenage movie, but that would miss something fundamental about Singleton's achievement. These young men have the same ambitions and insecurities as teenagers anywhere else. The difference is that their mistakes can carry devastating consequences, and their opportunities aren't remotely equal. Singleton refuses to reduce his characters to symbols, making their relationships feel painfully genuine. It's an essential coming-of-age story for mature audiences, and its portrayal of American adolescence remains painfully relevant.

Before podcasts gave everybody a microphone, Christian Slater was broadcasting teenage rebellion from his bedroom. In Allan Moyle's Pump Up the Volume, Slater plays Mark Hunter, an awkward high school student who transforms into the outspoken pirate radio personality Hard Harry after dark. His anonymous broadcasts become a sensation among classmates, particularly when he begins exposing the hypocrisy of the adults responsible for their education.

Slater is perfectly cast as a teenager who can barely hold a conversation in person but has plenty to say once nobody knows his identity. The movie occasionally gets carried away with its own rebellious spirit, yet its frustration with censorship and institutional dishonesty feels genuine. The soundtrack, featuring artists such as Concrete Blonde and the Pixies, is another excellent reason to seek it out. Pump Up the Volume belongs in any conversation about '90s youth culture because it understands how badly teenagers want to be heard, even when they're terrified of speaking up.

I grew up in New York City, and Kids still scares me because so much of it feels familiar. Larry Clark's controversial 1995 film follows a group of Manhattan teenagers over the course of a day as they wander through the city largely unsupervised. Written by a teenage Harmony Korine, it introduced audiences to young performers including Chloë Sevigny and Leo Fitzpatrick. The film's loose, almost documentary-like approach makes it feel less like a conventional drama than something you're witnessing from the sidewalk. That was the unsettling part for me. I recognized that world.

What makes Kids so disturbing isn't simply its depiction of adolescent recklessness. The film deals with HIV, sexual exploitation, and sexual violence, confronting viewers with consequences its characters seem frighteningly incapable of understanding. It's difficult to watch, and understandably controversial, but I have never thought of it as some far-fetched Hollywood nightmare. The streets were real. The sense of freedom was real. And the danger could be, too. This is certainly not a film for younger teenagers, but for mature audiences ready to confront its subject matter, Kids is among the most uncompromising portraits of adolescence the '90s ever produced.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Kids was considered THE MOVIE for rebellious teens. You had to watch it. That movie is highly exploitative. What he films with actual kids makes me uncomfortable now. Wassup Rockers is even worse. Every other movie had people that were of age playing younger kids. Kids opening scene was with a 12 to 13 year old and a 5 year old.

And I also prefer Class Act over House Party. But House Party is a classic. So are the rest on this list... besides Kids.

#3552. Captain America: The First Avenger's Director Was Supposed To Tackle A Much Bigger Marvel Hero

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In retrospect, Joe Johnston is an extremely important director in the history of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. After all, it was his "Captain America: The First Avenger" that found the MCU's emotional core and arguably its greatest hero upon its release in 2011, all while teeing up "The Avengers." The movie also served as our introduction to Chris Evans as Steve Rogers, who became a real anchor for this franchise. But before Johnston put his stamp on Cap, he nearly tackled a very different, and far bigger, Marvel superhero.

Prior to the MCU's success, Marvel sold off most of its character rights to various Hollywood studios. That's why Sony owns the movie rights to "Spider-Man" and the same reason why Universal Pictures holds the rights to the Incredible Hulk and solo films based on that character. In fact, the studio spent years developing a movie about the big green guy in the lead up to Ang Lee ("Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon") bringing "Hulk" to a theater near you in 2003.

Johnston, as it were, was among the filmmakers once set to helm a movie based on that very Marvel Comics character (as created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby). In a 1997 Variety report breaking down the "mania for Marvel" that was going on in Hollywood at the time, it was revealed that Johnston, coming off "Jumanji," was working on an "Incredible Hulk" feature film with screenwriter Jonathan Hensleigh ("Armageddon").

This was even before "Blade" became both a modest box office hit and one of the most important movies ever made, as it proved Marvel could deliver a mainstream success (and not just direct-to-video fare). Once "X-Men" hit in 2000, there was no longer any doubt. But back when Johnston was attached to his Hulk project, that wasn't the case.

As Variety reported in 1998, Jonathan Hensleigh was set to make his feature directorial debut on a Hulk movie before it was placed on the back burner. (By that point, the studio had already spent $20 million on development.) As for Joe Johnston, it's unclear why he departed the film, but he went on to direct "October Sky" and "Jurassic Park III" instead.

Even though "Hulk" was based on a very popular character, Ang Lee's movie was by no means a success. Against a budget of $137 million, it made just $245 million at the box office. Universal moved quickly after Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man" saved superhero movies from being just a fad, delivering record-breaking levels of success. It was the first film to ever make at least $100 million on a single weekend. That opened the floodgates.

Lee's "Hulk" didn't pan out commercially, but it's undeniable that Hulk himself was one of Marvel's most popular characters at that time. Captain America, as hard as it may be to fathom now, wasn't on the same level back then. It was in no small part thanks to Joe Johnston's work on "The First Avenger" that the tide changed. One year later, "The Avengers" became a box office hit that redefined blockbuster filmmaking. If Johnston's solo Cap movie hadn't worked, who knows if that big crossover would have panned out as well.

By MCU standards, "The First Avenger" was a modest success, pulling in $370 million at the box office. However, it's come to be regarded as one of the MCU's most underrated movies to date. That's largely thanks to Joe Johnston.

You can grab "Captain America: The First Avenger" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

#3551. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

#3550. Cillian Murphy's Critically Acclaimed 2025 Netflix Movie Flew Under Everyone's Radar

In 2025, Cillian Murphy played the harried head teacher of an English reform school who endures a day from hell while trying to keep his beleaguered institute from closing. It's one of his best recent performances. Sadly, the film went overlooked by mass audiences when it debuted on Netflix but is well worth seeking out.

If you've ever wondered how Murphy followed up the brilliant, horrifying, paradoxical biopic "Oppenheimer," you might be impressed to know that he did so with yet another critically-lauded effort. The Irish star previously worked with Belgian filmmaker Tim Mielants on the third season of "Peaky Blinders" before reuniting with him for the 2024 feature adaptation of Claire Keegan's "Small Things Like These." This was the first film starring Murphy to debut in the wake of his Oscar-winning performance in "Oppenheimer." and was about as good a follow-up as he could have hoped for.

"Small Things Like These" earned widespread critical praise and an impressive 94% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes. Re-teaming with Mielants for "Steve," then, seemed like an extremely sensible move for Murphy. Thankfully, that turned out to be the case. Author Max Porter adapted his own 2023 novella, "Shy," to create the screenplay for "Steve." The resulting film was almost as well received as "Small Things Like These," but didn't receive all that much recognition outside of the very respectable critical response. Thankfully, you can still watch it on Netflix.

Whereas "Shy" focuses on the eponymous student, "Steve" shifts its attention to, would you believe it, Steve. While Jay Lycurgo's Shy still plays a big role in the film, Cillian Murphy's resilient but struggling head teacher is the fulcrum around which the mid-90s-set film revolves.

He doesn't have an easy task. Steve oversees the fictional Stanton Wood, a government-funded reform school that's on the verge of closure in the wake of cuts to its funding — as evidenced by the crumbling manor house in which it operates. Meanwhile, the troubled youth attending Steve's school struggle to take advantage of what is essentially their last chance to turn their lives around and re-enter a society that has already decided it doesn't want them. One of these teens, Shy, describes himself as "angry and bored," and can't quite reconcile his self-destructive streak with his otherwise sensitive disposition.

Over the course of one particularly challenging day, during which a documentary crew arrives to chronicle the plight of Stanton Wood, we see Steve's own mental health decline in real time as the weight of his responsibilities overwhelms him. Privately struggling with addiction and lingering pain from past experiences, Murphy's educator finds himself on the verge of having to give up on the one thing that gives his life purpose.

If that sounds like a powerful drama, it is. Though not everybody was blown away by "Steve," the film still earned widespread praise for its portrait of a man trying to do good in the face of overwhelming odds and factors beyond his control. It was arguably one of the best streaming movies of 2025.

Cillian Murphy's best movies are some of the best movies of the last couple decades, with the Irish star always delivering memorable turns, even in films that struggled to match his talent ("Red Lights," Murphy's supernatural thriller with Robert De Niro was dead on arrival). But Murphy's naturalistic sensibility is particularly suited to the title role in "Steve," and even the critics who weren't convinced by the film itself had to concede as much.

"Steve" debuted at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival before being given a limited theatrical run in the United Kingdom and United States in September of that year. In October 2025, the film made its Netflix debut, by which time it had racked up a 77% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes. David Fear of Rolling Stone, however, wasn't too impressed. "It's handled in such a slapdash, klutzy manner," he wrote, "and feels so cut-rate, that you may find yourself raging alongside the movie's youngsters." John Anderson of the Wall Street Journal, however, sounded slightly concerned for viewers such as Fear. "If one isn't moved," he wrote in his review, "one should check one's pulse."

The Observer's Wendy Ide was with Anderson, writing, "'Steve' is gripping and exhausting, sharing common themes with Destin Daniel Cretton's 'Short Term 12' and Nora Fingscheidt's electrifying 'System Crasher.' But this film — and Murphy's devastating performance — exist in a class of their own." In his review for the Los Angeles Times, Robert Abele conceded that the film's "sentimental formula" was familiar but had to admit that Murphy delivered "another immersive portrayal of dark-hued, guilt-flecked intensity" in a film that "captures the electric hum of unpredictability and vulnerability." If you'd like to immerse yourself in that intensity, "Steve" is streaming on Netflix right now.

#3549. ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

For one of the most important screenings of “To Hold a Mountain,” the filmmakers had to bring their own electricity. In July, co-directors Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić hauled a tent, a generator, and a DCP up to the Montenegrin highlands where they had spent years filming.

The creative couple, also partnered in life, wanted the shepherds who lived and worked in Sinjajevina to see the movie they had made possible. But by then, Montenegro had already resolved their story’s central conflict — scrapping the government’s plan to turn these people’s ancestral pastures into a military training ground after joining NATO in 2017. Related Stories ‘You Can See Everything’ Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release

“To Hold a Mountain” won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize for documentary at Sundance, and Montenegro’s prime minister and president even showed up to the shepherds’ screening with their families, unannounced. When the film opens at New York’s Film Forum on December 16, American audiences will see the feature’s updated conclusion.

“We reopened the film to continue shooting and then a second end happened that was very empowering and powerful,” Tutorov said at IndieWire’s Art of the Doc series.

During our conversation, the filmmaker recalled arriving in Sinjajevina with Glomazić on the first day of protest. They wanted to help the community and make a movie, and agreed early on that those were two different jobs.

“We will separate our activist mission from our filmmaker’s mission,” she said. “That was a very good decision because it allowed us to be very bold in both roles.”

Onscreen, the fight over who would get to lay claim to the mountain centered on two people who already did: Gara, a shepherd and community leader, and Nada, the young girl she was raising. As the threat to their home brought a history of violence in their own family to the surface, the directors had to reckon with how much of Nada’s private life might become public.

“We really wanted it to be an empowering experience for [her],” Tutorov said.

Nada was twelve and a half when the filmmakers began to understand what the story would ask of her, and Tutorov said they decided to keep filming until she turned eighteen — precisely so Nada could decide for herself whether she wanted to be part of it. The crew logged more than 230 shooting days, though some yielded only half an hour of footage.

Gara and Nada had work to do, too. The directors and cinematographer Eva Kraljević shared a small shepherd’s shed, assisting with various chores including cows that had to be milked twice a day. Over successive summers, their routine became a framing device. Tutorov, who studied art history, thinks of the mountain as a kind of chorus bearing witness to living things on it.

Last July, just as the filmmakers were wrapping up, Montenegro’s government canceled the training-ground plan. Tutorov believes “To Hold a Mountain” and how it told the existing community’s story influenced that decision. She also pointed out that a different government was in power by 2025, following years of organizing by Sinjajevina locals.

At the shepherd’s screening a year later, Prime Minister Milojko Spajić said the film reinforced his view that canceling the plan had been the right call. Then Montenegro chose “To Hold a Mountain” as its official submission for the international feature Oscar. Tutorov said there was irony in realizing that, after years of fighting the government, she and Glomazić would be proudly representing the country on a global stage.

“It feels like they really kind of destroyed our strategy,” she said, warmly.

It’s a good joke, and an even better reason to remember that rough-and-tumble showing. For an evening, the people who’d spent years making their case to the government got to host its leaders on the very land they’d fought to keep. Tutorov recalled what Montenegro’s president told the filmmakers after seeing the movie: “Thank you guys for teaching us democracy.”

#3548. How Wuthering Waves Drives the Next Evolution of Anime Action RPGs

Fast combat, fluid traversal and Resonators who fight like themselves: how Wuthering Waves keeps raising the bar for anime action RPGs.

This article was produced in collaboration with our sponsor, Kuro Games.

When Wuthering Waves launched in May 2024, it arrived as one more open-world anime action RPG in a crowded field. Two years later, Version 3.7, "Prism's Illusion, Heart's Illumination", went live on September 30, 2026, closing the Xuanfang arc and adding two new Resonators, Hsin and Suoming. Kuro Games' title now sets the pace for the genre.

That reputation rests on four pillars: fast-paced combat, fluid movement and exploration, environments that keep evolving with every region, and compelling character presentation. Each one is strong on its own, but they also feed into each other and into the story.

In this article, we look at how these pillars connect, using examples from launch through Version 3.7, and why together they have raised what players expect from an anime action RPG. If you have never set foot on Solaris-3, there has never been a better time to start.

In Wuthering Waves, a weapon type is only the starting point. Every Resonator is officially classed as a Sword, Broadblade, Pistols, Gauntlets or Rectifier user, yet most of them fight with something that is uniquely theirs:

Roccia is a Gauntlets user, and her combat style is made even more distinctive by fighting alongside Pero, the mysterious magic box that serves as both prop and partner. Even her Intro Skill is called “Pero, Help.”

Aemeath is classed as a Sword user, but her kit revolves around switching into a mech form rooted in her past as an Exostrider Synchronist. The mech has its own attack chain, while Sync Strike: Armament Merge brings her two combat styles together.

Hsin is a Rectifier user who shifts between Answering Form and Illumining Form, with different attacks and action modules making transformation part of her rotation rather than a visual flourish.

The wider combat system supports that individuality. Players dodge, counter, use Echo Skills, manage each Resonator’s Forte Circuit, and switch characters in the middle of a combo. When Concerto Energy is ready, a switch can activate the outgoing Resonator’s Outro Skill and the incoming Resonator’s Intro Skill, turning a character change into a coordinated handoff of damage, buffs, healing, or positioning.

The basic rhythm is easy to understand, but there is room for more technical play. Experienced players can use what the community calls “swap-cancel,” switching during eligible animations to shorten rotations or layer actions from multiple Resonators. High-difficulty encounters further reward players for learning enemy patterns, judging counter windows, and deciding when to press an attack or dodge away. The same team can therefore feel simple in casual play and much more demanding when optimized.

Because combat moves so quickly, presentation must remain readable. Clear enemy wind-ups, distinctive intro animations, impact pauses, sound, and camera movement all help communicate what is happening. Hsin’s Answering and Illumining forms illustrate that balance: the transformation creates spectacle, but it also changes the structure and rhythm of her rotation. The visual climax and the mechanical decision are the same moment.

The attack style goes one step further: it tells you who the character is. Roccia's acrobatic flips and showy gestures come from her life as First Mate of the Fool's Troupe, a traveling performer of Rinascita's carnival scene. Aemeath’s singing carries her love of music into battle, while her mech form recalls her past as an Exostrider Synchronist.

The strongest character designs do more than look distinctive. Their animation, resources, and rotations all express the same personality, giving players another way to understand each Resonator through the rhythm of controlling them.

Wuthering Waves makes moving around Solaris-3 feel good, and that comfort is what lets the environment shine. Its foundation already includes sprinting, wall-running, climbing, gliding, and the Grapple. Later updates expanded that vocabulary:

Version 2.0 introduced Flight, giving the player a faster and more flexible way to move through Rinascita’s vertical spaces.

Rinascita’s transport Gondolas make Ragunna’s canals part of its traversal network. In Version 2.1’s Old Man and the Sea fishing activity, the Rover can also steer the Gondola Rachel through the waters around the Riccioli Islands.

Version 3.0 introduced the Expedition Motorbike, a system closely associated with the long routes and open terrain of Lahai-Roi.

Version 3.6 introduced sword-riding flight at specific quest locations in Xuanfang, giving the new region its own form of aerial traversal.

With travel this smooth, the journey becomes part of the fun rather than the gap between destinations. Instead of trudging toward the next waypoint, you sweep over rooftops and ridgelines, and you start noticing what lies below.

In Wuthering Waves, traversal is not bolted onto the map; the map design is inspired by it.

Rinascita’s canals, bridges, and rooftops work in harmony with Flight, helping the city feel like one connected space rather than a maze of streets. Lahai-Roi’s wide-open terrain offers a similarly natural fit for the motorbike. Roads connect resource points, while racetracks, motorbike challenges, and the ability to gather materials while riding make driving more than a way to get around; they make it part of exploration itself. Traversal and environment complement each other, reflecting a broader design approach that considers the player experience as a whole.

This relationship matters because the way players move changes how they read the landscape. A fast or flexible traversal system encourages exploration and detours: a rooftop becomes a route, a distant ridge becomes an invitation, and a vertical structure becomes something to circle rather than merely climb.

The environment stops being a backdrop for objectives and becomes space players come to understand through movement.

The environment is also full of puzzles, and each region solves them in its own way. Lahai-Roi has its Smartprint Cube puzzles, Echo-form puzzles ask you to transform into an Echo to reach a solution, and ice-cube puzzles have you shifting blocks to open the way forward. Other activities use movement, object manipulation, or region-specific rules to redirect the player away from the main path.

The rewards vary, but many chests, exploration milestones, and activities contribute Astrite or other progression materials. More importantly, the puzzles reward curiosity itself, encouraging players to follow detours, investigate anything unusual, and explore beyond the main route.

Good traversal gets the player to a location. Good environmental design rewards them for looking closer.

Connecting story and gameplay means more than placing a battle between two cutscenes. Narrative, combat, level-design, and animation teams must agree early on what a character or chapter is fundamentally about. When that alignment works, dialogue, combat rotations, puzzles, and the environment can all speak the same design language.

Kuro Games builds this alignment around each character’s core concept. Cartethyia’s “three swords as one” is reflected in both her story and combat identity, while the sun-and-moon imagery surrounding Augusta and Luno connects their identity to their battle presentation. Frequent communication between teams allows an idea discovered in one area to echo in another, whether players encounter it first in a quest or in a character’s kit.

Version 2.2 provides a clear example. The Rover accompanies Cartethyia through a series of gameplay sequences in the Inverted Tower before finally reaching Fleurdelys. Here, the gameplay is closely integrated with Cartethyia’s abilities and story. The concept of her three swords is echoed in an objective that asks players to set three swords into three locations across Avinoleum to lift the final seal. The battle sequence involving Cadanto likewise reflects the guardian-knight bond between Cartethyia and Cadanto, while the Inverted Tower design gives physical form to the opposing aspects represented by Cartethyia and Fleurdelys. Together, these elements give the entire sequence a unified feel.

Making that integration work also requires careful control of pacing. Main Quests cannot always play like endgame challenges, because excessive difficulty can interrupt a scene’s emotional flow. By emphasizing interaction, feedback, and narrative expression, the gameplay supports the story rather than competing with it. Character mechanics express identity, objectives turn lore into action, and architecture gives relationships a physical form. The result is not merely a story interrupted by gameplay, but a story the player helps perform.

What makes Wuthering Waves stand out is not one great update but a steady run of them. Across 23 version releases since launch, Kuro Games has delivered more than 100 hours of main-story content, over 200 square kilometers of open-world maps, 206 distinct enemy types, and 67 playable Resonators. Every major version has pushed the world and its possibilities a little further.

The clearest example was this summer’s Cyberpunk: Edgerunners collaboration. It brought Lucy and Rebecca into Wuthering Waves alongside two Cyberpunk-themed areas, Night City and the Moon, and a Nightmare: Adam Smasher boss encounter. Its emotional coda led many fans to nickname it “Edgerunners Episode 11.” CD Projekt Red associate game director Paweł Sasko summed up the response: “We have done a bunch of collabs in the past, small and huge, and I have never seen a response this insane from the community.”

Version 3.4, which featured the collaboration, also set a new Steam concurrent-player peak for Wuthering Waves. Across 2026, the game repeatedly reached No. 1 on Steam’s Top Sellers charts in major markets, and its latest update, Version 3.7, continued that performance by taking the global top spot on launch day. That momentum has translated into formal recognition as well: a Still Playing – Mobile nomination at the 2026 Golden Joystick Awards, plus Best Ongoing Game and Popular Vote at the Thailand Game Awards, where Kuro Games was also named Best Game Publisher; and three nominations at the 17th Hollywood Music in Media Awards in 2026, across Song – Video Game (Console & PC), Song/Score – Mobile Video Game, and Live Concert for Visual Media.

With Version 3.8 now approaching, Kuro Games is not slowing down. For anyone wondering where the anime action RPG goes next, Solaris-3 is a good place to look. Kuro has done it again—and the next step is already on the way.

#3547. 51 Years Later, Jaws' Most Famous Line Is Still The Greatest Quote In Movie History

How many movies can you name that inspire such a massive, visceral reaction with such a minimalist approach? "Jaws" stands on an island unto itself in this regard, practically since the moment the blockbuster-defining hit first made landfall in 1975. The one-word title alone is a stroke of genius, standing in stark contrast to clunky word salads that studios tend to go with these days (usually followed by an obnoxious subtitle of some kind, naturally). John Williams' iconic score and that famous two-note theme quite literally speak for themselves, evoking a sense of dread and menace that would've been lost amid a more overbearing arrangement.

But most of all, despite including a barnburner monologue or two, let's just say there's a reason why one of the simplest and most straightforward lines of all has gone on to become arguably the most famous quote in cinema history. Of course, we're talking about actor Roy Scheider's pitch-perfect portrayal of police chief Martin Brody's moment of realization out at sea: "You're gonna need a bigger boat." Celebrated and parodied and recreated countless times since in pop culture, this one piece of dialogue towers above all the rest.

It's fun to imagine those in the theater on opening day actually feeling their moviegoing reality shift around them during this scene, just as the action in "Jaws" itself shifted into another gear entirely. The truth is, however, this was one of those singular moments in cinema that needed time and perspective to fully appreciate. It's not hyperbolic in the least to state that everything changed after this, in ways that are still reverberating today. Over 50 years later, it's as good a time as any to look back and appreciate the greatest quote of them all.

"You're gonna need a bigger boat." — Martin Brody

Have six total words ever encapsulated so many primal emotions? We're not exactly reinventing the wheel to propose that "Jaws" taps into an instinctive fear of the unknown and the horrors of nature, lurking just outside our comfortable existence. Despite how high we rise and how far our greedy ambitions take us, we're still fragile beings at the mercy of forces beyond our control — whether it's hapless swimmers trying to enjoy summer vacation, or, say, a certain mayor of Amity Island concerned solely about tourism profits over public safety. And when a killer apex predator is on the prowl, well, not even a shark hunter's boat is enough to keep us safe in unfamiliar waters.

That's the psychoanalyzing version of events, at least. While sitting down to experience "Jaws" for the umpteenth re-watch (or even for the very first time), what sticks out the most in this classic scene is just how terrified everyone is once they finally catch a glimpse of their quarry. Even Robert Shaw's cold-blooded Quint, a man who's seen and survived the worst, is visibly taken aback by the sight of a gigantic dorsal fin breaching the surface. In the moment, this isn't an existential concern about humanity's place in the food chain. This is pure survival, plain and simple.

Amusingly enough, there's another alternate explanation behind this legendary line. In a now-famous production story, it's been revealed that this was actually an improvised insult aimed squarely at penny-pinching producers. As co-writer Carl Gottlieb explained, "['You're gonna need a bigger boat'] became a catchphrase for anytime anything went wrong." With that added layer of irony, it's no wonder this quote took on a life of its own.

#3544. Ink Review: Danny Boyle's Tabloid Media Origin Story Will Make You Feel Sick

Journalism and media have undergone significant changes in the 21st century. The internet has altered everything and barriers are gone. The gatekeepers who used to be there to say what was or wasn't news don't exist, at least not in the way they used to. Director Danny Boyle has examined this "Give 'em what they want" tabloid media culture in his latest movie "Ink," which will make anyone who values real journalism sick to their stomach.

Adapting the play of the same name, the movie traces the origins of the British gossip rag The Sun, focusing on a group of misfit visionaries who had an idea for a new kind of news. Rather than simply report "the news," why not give people what they want instead?

Less a biopic a about Rupert Murdoch (played here by Guy Pearce) and his family, the real-life family the Roy clan on "Succession" is based off of, it focuses instead largely on Larry Lamb, played by "Sinners" star Jack O'Connell. Lamb was the man hand-picked by Murdoch to change The Sun from a fledgling paper into something, well, different. Driven by revenge and a sense of "I'll show 'em," Lamb, at least as presented by Boyle, is one of the most significant figures who shaped the modern era. And not in a good way, it probably goes without saying. But I'll say it anyway.

The story being told in "Ink" is an ugly one with grave consequences in the real world. Danny Boyle starts out by making this seem almost fun and exciting. Larry Lamb assembling his team has an "Ocean's Eleven" quality to it, with the kinetic energy of some of the director's best movies, most notably "Trainspotting."

Slowly but surely though, it all devolves into something more sinister. Even though news and journalism should probably be seen as a public good and an essential function of any democratic society, the need to make these publications profitable changes the game. Lamb and Rupert Murdoch lean into the "business" side of the news business, and that's where things get downright icky.

The tone of "Ink" shifts from a fun outsider tale to a dark story about taking something too far in pursuit of capitalist superiority. We see Larry Lamb lose the man he was, becoming a man that's difficult to respect. While the great newsroom movies in cinema history, such as "All the President's Men" and "Spotlight," make viewers feel the power of journalism, "Ink" forces the viewer to understand that power can and often is used in far less noble ways. Boyle is offering up his view of the men responsible for that shift.

By heading back to the past, namely the late '60s in the U.K., Boyle shines a light on the modern era. Podcasts. Blogs. Tabloids. Cable news. It all traces its roots back to this moment in history and it's hard not to leave this movie feeling some kind of way about our current media culture.

"Ink" also makes the viewer think about how accurate movies like "Spotlight" and other "based on a true story" movies are. Boyle and writer James Graham probably weren't too interested in getting everything exactly right, as this movie is about how a narrative can be shaped. Boyle and Graham shaped a narrative using real people who had real influence on the world as we know it. Accuracy isn't the point. It's about painting a picture.

"Ink" is a true showcase for Jack O'Connell. He's chewed the screen rather delightfully in movies like "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple" in recent years. But this film allows him to be more human and take the driver's seat in a grounded movie with a killer ensemble. He's the best part of a movie that also includes an excellent Claire Foy and a good-as-ever Guy Pearce.

Pearce, in particular, deserves credit for playing Rupert Murdoch with nuance. It would be easy to turn the guy who helped create Fox News into a cigar-chomping, cartoonish villain. Pearce didn't take the easy way out.

Will "Ink" rank amongst Danny Boyle's best films? Maybe not. It's tonally uneven and about as subtle as a jackhammer. But it's also got one hell of a point to make. News is kind of like vegetables: Not the most fun, but nutritious and necessary. "Ink" shines an uncomfortable light on how we, as a society, allowed news to turn from vegetables into junk food. Eat enough junk food, you'll get sick.

"Ink" hits select theatres December 11, 2026, before releasing on Netflix on January 8, 2027.

#3543. ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Grasshopper Film releases “Zi” in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

A Hong Kong violinist who’s losing her grip on reality, young Zi (Michelle Mao) is haunted by visions of her future self. The doctors at the local neurology center suspect that she might be suffering from the early symptoms of a brain tumor, but Zi — a being of pure cinema, cobbled together from the half-formed memories of films like “La Jetée” and “Cléo from 5 to 7” — will have to wait a long and lonely 24 hours for the test results to come back.  Related Stories ‘You Can See Everything’ Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release

Well, maybe not so lonely. Crying on one of the innumerable concrete steps that climb Lantau Island, Zi is consoled by a sweet American expat with a strangely familiar face (and an aggressively unnatural blonde wig). Her name is L, she’s a disillusioned former dancer played by the luminous Haley Lu Richardson, and she can’t help but reciprocate the inexplicable closeness that Zi feels towards her. Over the course of a single night together, these two lost souls will help to relocate each other in time — to resynchronize with the world around them, reconnect with the infinite potential of the present, and return themselves to the creative purpose that once anchored them to it.

Even if seen without a shred of context, it would be obvious to anyone that “Zi” was made by someone who is — or hopefully was — desperate to spark a realignment of his own. To steal himself away from regret and anxiety and tether his perspective back to the now. Shot without a script or a budget in the immediate aftermath of Kogonada’s ill-received “A Big Bold Beautiful Journey” (the “After Yang” auteur’s studio debut, by all indications a soul-crushing experience for an artist whose two previous features retained the delicate grace of the video essays that he used to make), this searching and unformed wisp of an experiment hardly represents the first time that an ascendent director has scaled down after a misstep, but “Zi” takes the notion of “one for me” to much greater and more galvanizing extremes than usual.

This isn’t just a filmmaker trying to get back on track, it’s a filmmaker desperately, nakedly searching for a way to fall back in love with filmmaking itself. A way to prove that it might still love him back. (Kogonada described the project to IndieWire as “A retreat, as well as a pursuit.”)

While the prospect of watching Kogonada do that will naturally be of greater interest to those who have watched him get to this point, this movie’s palpably improvised nature — its stolen shots and recursive shape lend the impression of someone trying to cut their ultra-evocative vacation footage into a coherent narrative — would force anyone to wonder about the meta-textual aspects of its creation. “You feel like your sole purpose in life is something, and it doesn’t choose you back,” L sputters out at one point. “What do you do with that? I had to get away from it all. That’s why I came here. Wandering.”

Since arriving in Hong Kong, she’s made a habit of collecting sounds in much the same way as Kogonada has come there on the hunt for images. They both find a dissonance around Victoria Harbor that reflects their internal feelings of otherness and self-alienation. It’s China, but not. It’s a single city, but one split across two main areas by a stretch of the sea that some people never cross. It’s among the world’s most densely populated metropolises, but the vertical terrain seems fundamentally inhospitable to human civilization, and nature continues to assert itself between every skyscraper, shopping mansion, and crack in the sidewalk. Zi is the only native character in the film, but the history and design of Hong Kong reflects her disassociation as well — like her, the former British colony’s experience of the present is delayed.

That’s the closest thing to a diagnosis we get for what ails her, though it’s clear that Kogonada is leaning more towards soft science-fiction than the stuff of hard medicine. “Temoral relativism” is how L’s ex-fiancé Min (Jin Ha) describes it, though he’s slow to reveal how much he knows about Zi’s condition. Everything she perceives is already in the past. I suppose that’s true for all of us to some degree, if you factor in the nanoseconds that elapse between stimuli and our ability to perceive it, but the situation is more pronounced for Zi (who Mao plays with the effervescent helplessness of a paper airplane). Of course, that doesn’t explain why she believes she’s bearing witness to visions of her future self, but that confusion only exacerbates her feelings of distance from the present.

Even in its more platonic dimensions, the threadbare story that gradually allows Zi to close that gap is awash with the romance of loss, reconciliation, and belonging. Kogonada is falling back in love with the movies right before our eyes, and yet,  in characteristic fashion, that process isn’t garish or forced. His is a vision that is revealed through careful subtraction — by clearing away all of the dust and smudges that came to obscure it.

While Kogonada indulges in a few legible winks to his cinematic forebears (the most obvious of those being a step-printed homage to Wong Kar Wai, and my most far-fetched being a disoriented nod to José Luis Guerín’s “In the City of Sylvia”), he and cinematographer Benjamin Loeb almost completely eschew the neon exoticism that foreigners tend to look for in Hong Kong, with the vast majority of the film being captured in unfussy handheld shots that accentuate its here-and-now anxiety and delegate the emotional heavy lifting to an impeccably curated soundtrack of Ryuichi Sakamoto remixes and originals.

By the end, “Zi” engenders a certain emotional attachment toward and between its characters, all of it building to a gently unexpected gutpunch of a final minute. But even that last-minute reveal — not a plot twist so much as a sudden change in perspective — is rooted more in the movie’s form than its plot, as Kogonada’s characters remain largely symbolic of their function in the writer-director’s journey back to himself.

It’s a testament to Mao, Ha, and especially Richardson — who continues to be so good at grounding Kogonada’s most abstract ideas in a tender human place — that “Zi” retains even a soft dramatic pull as it searches for the present, though its recursive nature certainly wasn’t conceived with a casual audience in mind. If you’re hooked, which I wasn’t, or haunted by it, which I was, that will likely have less to do with an acute emotional connection to these characters than with the overflowing rewards of watching someone rediscover the sound of their own voice, and hear a way forward into the future in its echoes.

“Zi” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Grasshopper Film releases it in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

Make sure you’re not being redirected to the Kindle or Amazon mobile application, because you won't see the free book option there; instead, use your internet browser on your phone or computer.

Make sure you’re not clicking the ”Pre-order for...” button, as that will direct you to pay. The preloaded files also gave some much-needed insight into what Rockstar has in store for GTA 6 on PS5 Pro. The files appear to reference 120Hz support, which wouldn't be too surprising for a game on the more-powerful version of Sony's console. Klara and the Sun has been enshrouded by darkness.

The new sci-fi movie, which was directed and co-written by Taika Waititi, is an adaptation of the Kazuo Ishiguro novel of the same name that follows Klara (Jenna Ortega), an out-of-date Artificial Friend who is purchased by a rural family and tries to improve their lives. After debuting on October 23 with an underwhelming domestic gross of $701,059, 2026's Klara and the Sun dropped 77.5% during its sophomore weekend (in which Sony had already stopped reporting its box office numbers, as it was not a Top 10 contender), which marked the 85th worst sophomore drop in history.

While Klara and the Sun is still playing in a number of theaters nationwide (there is at least one showtime listed this week at the AMC Orange 30 in Southern California), Fandango shows no showtimes in or around many major domestic markets, including New York City, Chicago, Boston, Dallas, Newark, Minneapolis, Seattle, Portland, Kansas City, and Cleveland. However, it is unknown exactly how many theaters are playing the movie or how much it has made at the box office this weekend.

Klara and the Sun's week 3 numbers have not appeared on the domestic weekend charts on either The Numbers or Box Office Mojo. This is likely because its numbers are low enough that they are negligible. Movies playing in very few theaters, either in limited release or toward the tail end of their theatrical run, do not always have their box office reported, either by distributors or rivals. This was the case earlier this year with the Connor Storrie sci-fi movie April X, which had a small specialty release this October but has a blank listing on both sources.

If the Taika Waititi movie had a similar drop this weekend as it had last weekend, it would have earned roughly $35,000 at the domestic box office, landing it at No. 32 on the chart for the weekend. However, given the fact that it is absent from many markets, it likely earned less than that.

There are 34 movies on the domestic chart for the weekend of November 6.

If Klara and the Sun's week 3 grosses are truly negligible, then the movie's final global gross has likely settled around the number it hit by the end of Thursday, November 5, which was $2.643 million. This cements the movie's status as a theatrical bomb. While it had a relatively slim reported budget of $20 million, the movie most likely needs to have earned roughly $50 million in order to break even in theaters, which is a total it got nowhere near earning in theaters.

#3539. Every Martin McDonagh-Directed Movie, Ranked (Including Wild Horse Nine)

British-Irish filmmaker Martin McDonagh has become one of cinema's foremost stewards of the tragicomedy. In a McDonagh movie, violence or death can be hilarious, or devastating, or both. He forces us to sympathize with unlikable or even evil characters by showing that even those bad eggs still have human sides. Catholicism casts its shadow over McDonagh's stories, especially in how he loves to focus on guilty, even suicidally guilty, people. He dares you to sympathize with those guilty people in spite of their horrible sins and, quite often, he succeeds.

While there are usually glimmers of hope for redemption, McDonagh's stories never end with tidy answers, either. As for his crackling dialogue, it's remarkable how adept he is at both non-sequiturs and rhythmic back-and-forth. If Quentin Tarantino had been raised in London and Galway instead of Tennessee and Los Angeles, you'd have a writer like Martin McDonagh.

McDonagh began as a playwright, producing several plays in the 1990s and early 2000s. He moved into film in 2004 with his directed short, "Six Shooter," and then jumped to features with 2008's "In Bruges." He's remained there since and has become a frequent Oscar nominee to boot. To celebrate his sixth and latest film "Wild Horse Nine" hitting theaters, here are all of McDonagh's movies, ranked!

McDonagh's first film was a short one: 2004's "Six Shooter," which is available to watch for free on YouTube. In 2006, "Six Shooter" received an Academy Award for Best Live Action Short Film. It's the least of McDonagh's films by its very nature as a short, but running only 26 minutes has a positive double-edge: The script is small but airtight, like a great short story should be.

Brendan Gleeson plays Donnelly, an Irish man taking a train ride after his wife died in the hospital that morning. There's also a couple (David Wilmot and Aisling O'Sullivan) onboard reeling from the death of their infant son, as well as a very rude and loud kid (Rúaidhrí Conroy). The kid enjoys running his mouth and prodding the other passengers, and rest assured, he's holding a dark secret too.

Even with its short runtime, "Six Shooter" still has a lot of what have become McDonagh's trademarks as a storyteller. There's a death scene that'll make you jump with how abrupt it is, as well as an overall theme of grief-driven people looking to suicide for the answer. There's also a twist, seeded offhandedly in the movie's opening, that comes back and completely reframes everything at the end.

Considering the accolades "Six Shooter" earned, all the way up to the Academy, it's also a credit to McDonagh that he hasn't remade it as a full-length feature. The train ride setting benefits from the brevity, and while the twist is satisfying at 20 minutes of build-up, at 90 it might be a drag. "Six Shooter" sits well enough as is.

In "Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri," McDonagh wrote a story about a tight-knit community in the vein of several of his plays. But as you can guess from the title, this one takes place in small town America, not rural Ireland. Whether McDonagh succeeded in his self-imposed challenge of setting with "Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri" still splits audiences.

Mildred Hayes (Frances McDormand, who won Best Actress for the performance) is a woman grieving the still-unsolved rape and murder of her daughter, Angela (Kathryn Newton). To apply some pressure to police chief Bill Willoughby (Woody Harrelson), she puts up three billboards outside the town that read, in succession: "Raped While Dying." "And Still No Arrests?" "How Come, Chief Willoughby?" Mildred turns her grief into a spectacle the town can't look away from.

Upon wide release, "Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri" attracted a vocal backlash alongside its accolades. The main lightning rod was the character Jason Dixon (Sam Rockwell), a racist police officer accused of torturing a Black suspect, who attempts a soulful redemption arc. Many found that approach in poor taste; Dixon doesn't repent his bigotry, but the film insists he has a heart in spite of it.

McDonagh has said he did not intend "Three Billboards" as a message movie about American politics, and he's definitely not the type of writer who uses his characters to deliver moralistic lectures. The easy answer is that McDonagh was a little careless about adding local color to the kind of story he's written about Irish villages before. Mixed with his predilection for asking audiences to sympathize with immoral people, that approach landed the wrong way for many. McDonagh's settings usually feel whimsical, like black comedy fairy tales, and that doesn't quite mesh with politically potent themes.

Two of McDonagh's most frequent leading men are Colin Farrell and Sam Rockwell, but he's only used them together in one movie: his third film, and second feature, "Seven Psychopaths," which is a much stranger, more contemplative movie than its violent-sounding title suggests. McDonagh's most structurally ambitious movie, "Seven Psychopaths" is Spike Jonze and Charlie Kaufman's "Adaptation" by way of Quentin Tarantino.

Farrell plays Marty, a writer's block-afflicted screenwriter working on his new script "Seven Psychopaths." He's also best friends with a criminal, Billy (Rockwell), who gets himself in hot water after kidnapping mob boss Charlie Costello's (Woody Harrelson) dog and sleeping with Costello's girlfriend, Angela (Olga Kurylenko).

As Marty, Billy, and Billy's partner-in-crime Hans (Christopher Walken) drive away fleeing the gangsters, the movie tips its hand. Marty suggests that, in his "Seven Psychopaths" script, "the first hour should be like a perfect set-up for an out-and-out revenge flick." But then the leads should "walk away" and just go out to the dessert and talk like real people. Billy is dumbfounded ("No shootouts?!"), but lo and behold, that's what the actual "Seven Psychopaths" you're watching does.

The movie's meta approach lets McDonagh engage in some amusing self-criticism. "Your women characters are awful," Hans tells Marty. Marty, not even trying to deny it, just answers that "it's a hard world for women." There are also layered interludes demonstrating Marty's ideas for his screenplay, like a former Viet Cong soldier (Long Nguyen) on a vengeance quest.

Your mileage with "Seven Psychopaths" will depend heavily on your tolerance for metafiction. But if you can get on its wavelength, it's a very funny movie with three excellently played leads.

As a filmmaker settles into their career, there's always the risk they'll start going through the motions, i.e. making films that only echo what they've said or accomplished in previous, better films. I mention this because McDonagh's latest film "Wild Horse Nine" has the exact same essential premise as "In Bruges" — two professional murderers on holiday where one has been tasked with killing the other.

In 1973, Chris (John Malkovich) and Lee (Sam Rockwell) are CIA agents working in Santiago, Chile to undermine the country's democracy and bring dictator Augusto Pinochet to power. They take a vacation to Easter Island; Chris is dying of cancer, and he wants Lee to kill him in a peaceful place. Their boss, MJ (Steve Buscemi), is worried because Chris is talking about penning memoirs and sharing the CIA's darkest secrets.

This is both Malkovich and Buscemi's first time working with McDonagh, and both actors take to his dialogue easily. Malkovich is perfectly cast as the airy and impish Chris, just as Buscemi brings his tightly wound Mr. Pink from "Reservoir Dogs" energy to MJ. "Old killer haunted by his past" is nothing new, but Chris isn't broody and self-flagellating even though he is suffering Catholic guilt. He's more like the eccentric grandfather who says what's on his mind because he's aged past caring about consequences.

The first chunk of "Wild Horse Nine" is a little uneventful, as Lee and Chris tour Easter Island and bicker. But the same could be said of "In Bruges," so I should've trusted the process. The movie's emotional arcs and its mysteries come together beautifully in the second half. It's also politically sharper, or at least angrier, than "Three Billboards." If you want to hear how America supposedly "protects democracy" across the world, watch something else.

"Breaking up" with a longtime friend can be just as painful as ending a romantic relationship. Don't believe me? Then live a little, but before that, also go and watch "The Banshees of Inisherin," the definitive and brutal friend breakup movie.

In 1994, McDonagh tried to write a play titled "The Banshees of Inisheer," but couldn't crack it. He hung onto the title, and years later he found a story for which to use it (albeit tweaked to reflect the change from the real Irish island Inisheer to the fictional Inisherin). Set in the 1920s, "Banshees" follows two former lifelong friends, farmer Pádraic (Colin Farrell) and fiddle player Colm (Brendan Gleeson).

Colm decides one day he doesn't want to be friends anymore. Unlike your typical movie feud, there's no real inciting incident. Pádraic is a nice guy, but boring, and so Colm — who's in a midlife crisis and wants to write a musical composition that history will remember — doesn't want to speak to him any more. You can tell they've been friends because of convenience first: It's a small island and they have little else in their lives. Since Pádraic didn't do anything wrong, there's no real way to repair their friendship, and attempts at reconciliation eventually beget revenge.

Farrell and Gleeson's casting carries extra weight considering they starred together in McDonagh's "In Bruges." That film was about their characters' saving each other through their friendship, whereas this one is about them hurting each other as a friendship dissolves. Farrell's puppy dog face is perfect for the spurned and confused Pádraic, while Gleeson's turns his usual jovial presence as cold as Inisherin's ocean winds. The virtual third player is Kerry Condon as Pádraic's sister Siobhán, the exasperated straight woman of Inisherin.

"In Bruges" holds a special place in my film-loving heart. I saw it when I was about 14 years old, and, as a Catholic school alum just beginning to love Quentin Tarantino, I was perfectly primed for it to floor me. I still remember it as a pivotal moment in my journey as a cinephile and it holds up as McDonagh's most effective, perfectly-executed movie.

Ray (Colin Farrell) and his mentor Ken (Brendan Gleeson) are two British-Irish hitmen sent to hide out in a Belgian city, Bruges, and await instruction from their boss Harry (Ralph Fiennes). Ken loves the town's old-fashioned charm and the sight-seeing, but Ray is irritable and makes it clear Bruges is the last place he wants to be.

What seems like a buddy comedy reveals itself as a devastating drama when we find out why the pair are in Bruges. During their previous job (Ray's first), a little boy died as collateral damage. It was an accident, yes, but it still only happened because Ray shot up a priest (Ciarán Hinds) by ambushing him in a confessional. So, yeah, can't imagine the good Lord will be looking too kindly on that! Ray has to rediscover the will to live, and Ken — who'd been assigned by Harry to kill Ray as punishment for killing the kid — is his unlikely guardian angel.

From the character arcs to the tone (which remains frequently funny even after we get the devastating truth), "In Bruges" is a writing masterclass elevated even higher by three perfectly in-tune performances. Ray's redemption was echoed off-screen, too. Colin Farrell taking on such a complex and morally compromised but still empathetic character let him prove what a great actor he is after a rough few years prior.

#3538. How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying

No one is doing monster movies quite like director Takashi Yamazaki and his team — who not once but twice now, with “Godzilla Minus One” and “Godzilla Minus Zero,” have made Godzilla feel both bigger than Tokyo Bay and extremely emotional and personal, even handcrafted. Much of that comes down to the narrative balance between our human heroes and the King of the Monsters, of course. But it’s also about the grounded, physical ways the monsters are brought to life.

Much has already been made of the fact that both Godzilla’s and King Ghidorah’s roars were recorded by blasting the sound effects against real physical spaces (and probably scaring some hikers in the process) so we wouldn’t just hear something otherworldly. We’d hear the texture of the loudspeakers, the reverberation of the sound on the concrete of a dam (for Ghidorah) or a dome (for Godzilla) — the unreal brought into a real, physical space. Related Stories ‘You Can See Everything’ Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release

But that is only the light-up blue tip of the kaiju for the work done by the “Godzilla Minus Zero” sound design team. Sound designer Natsuko Inoue and production and post-production sound mixer Hisafumi Takeuchi constantly found ways to tie the most fantastical moments back to Earth, because that sonic believability keeps the audience invested in the action.

“ When audiences hear sounds that they’ve never heard before too frequently, I think it removes you from the world because it’s too foreign and it’ll stand out,” Inoue told IndieWire. “Once a fantasy-like or fictitious sound goes through the sort of real-world echo, then it becomes a lot more palatable, or we become more receptive to how it sounds because it’s echoing in a way that we recognize. So that was a way that we really tied the visuals to the sound and made it feel more grounded.”

This grounding process is especially important, and especially challenging, when things that should be on the ground take to the air as a part of Ghidorah’s gravity beam. Inoue did an initial pass of the sound effect for the beam that allows Ghidorah to throw whole houses up in the air high enough for our favorite eternally tormented, former Kamikaze pilot Kôichi Skikishima (Ryûnosuke Kamiki) to fly past them. But it wasn’t quite right.

“So I went back into the Foley studio, and I wanted to capture that feeling of something being lifted and rising. I took this very small speaker, and I placed it right next to a bunch of different objects — a sheet of metal or some wood or a water tank — to capture a sound that almost felt distorted,” Inoue said.

That distortion, bounced off different types of objects, captured the sensation Inoue was after: the sonic equivalent of your stomach lifting into your mouth.

“Oftentimes in sound design, when you layer too many sounds or put too much processing on it, it starts to ruin the original material or the original sound that you’ve captured. So this distortion became a very strong foundation. I didn’t add too much post-processing on it,” Inoue said.

What she did do was hand it over to Takeuchi to create the sense of whole blocks caught up in Ghidorah’s gravity beam and preserve the dialogue and add background dialogue, so that we’re always afraid for the human beings in danger during Ghidorah’s rampages.

When Shikishima first flies through Ghidorah’s gravity beam, the sound team really wanted to lean into the character’s emotional response to something that’s mindbendingly horrible. “I added a Doppler effect — so like when an ambulance or a police car drives by and the sound shifts slightly — [to give] the sensation that you’re passing through,” Takeuchi told IndieWire.

It’s that shifting of sound, more than any one particular sound, that adds a scale to the horror beyond what Shikishima or what we can see. “We wanted to be very mindful of the balance and what it was doing and what it was supposed to do for each scene,” Takeuchi said.

“What we were trying to do is take sounds that you would hear in nature and then design and add to it in almost like an extension type of way, and that’s how we make the Kaiju as well as the gravity beam feel more real,” Inoue added.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now playing in theaters.
