#3537. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

#3536. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Will Have Some Unexpected Main Characters [Exclusive]

Don't let the title fool you: "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" may suggest that this Prime Video series is all about the origins of Sauron (played by Charlie Vickers), but the truth is much more complicated than that. In the very first scene of Season 1, we see the events of the saga told through the eyes of Galadriel (Morfyyd Clark), positioning her as our de facto main protagonist. In the time since, an ensemble of characters have risen up to take the reins of this story. There's Robert Aramayo's Elrond, the Dwarf king Durin (Owain Arthur), our lovable clan of Harfoots, and so many more spread out over the vast expanse of Middle-earth. But, if you ask the show's creative team, Season 3 takes this versatile approach to even greater heights.

In fact, I did ask them exactly that. At the recent press junket for "The Rings of Power," I spoke to co-showrunner Patrick McKay about whether he sees these three seasons as a Sauron-centric narrative or something that extends far beyond our favorite Dark Lord. According to McKay, it's a tricky balance:

"Sauron is going to be the center of gravity in many ways, but it's an ensemble show, and we love the idea that from episode to episode, sequence to sequence, someone might surprise you [...] We love that we can do that."

McKay actually singled out one particular character by name who takes the lead at one point in "The Rings of Power" Season 3, but we'll save that (very minor) reveal for below. Needless to say, it's a perfect example of the series' writers staying light on their feet. With such a talented cast, the show might as well use them to its advantage.

Without spoiling any specifics, one of the more memorable instances of this comes in the early episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3. While Sauron's ongoing conquest of Middle-earth puts the pressure on the forces of good, the sequestered island nation of Númenor is dealing with its own troubles closer to home. Caught in the middle of this turmoil, the family made up of Isildur (Maxim Baldry), his sister Eärien (Ema Horvath), and their father Elendil (Lloyd Owen) are hard-pressed to keep up a united front. This subplot may not be the most obvious favorite for many viewers of the show, but Season 3 goes out of its way to shine a brighter spotlight on one secondary character in particular.

According to Patrick McKay, fans ought to be on the lookout for what Episode 2 has in store. "The second episode this season, arguably the protagonist is Ema Horvath's character Eärien over in Númenor — who you abstractly would never think that the sister of the [character] over in that particular story would take that kind of prominence," he explained. It's a calculated gamble, but one that speaks to his and co-showrunner J.D. Payne's new mentality. McKay added:

"We're just looking [for] ways to shake it up and surprise you, and we know what Ema can do. And we were very excited to give her that chance."

The storylines revolving around Galadriel, Sauron, and Jamie Campbell Bower's newly-introduced Celeborn will likely make most of the headlines this year, but don't sleep on the supporting characters populating this world. You never know which one might surprise you. "The Rings of Power" Season 3 premieres November 11, 2026, on Prime Video.

#3535. Letterboxd’s Sale to the New York Times: 9 Pros, Cons, and Big Questions from the $330 Million Deal

After several months of business talks and speculation, Letterboxd is about to have new owners. The New York Times is closing in on deal to acquire the film-logging social media platform, which values the company at $330 million. It’s an eye-popping increase from 2023, when the Canadian holding company Tiny bought a majority stake at a $50 million valuation.

Far beyond the film industry, there is a dismal track record and daunting uncertainty when it comes to companies’ ability to maintain their identities after being acquired. Social media reception to the pending New York Times deal generally peaked at resigned relief (“the best case scenario” was a common refrain) while also drawing more cynical, even existential responses about the future of Letterboxd. As the website’s user base holds its breath over the future, these are some pros, cons, and big unknowns to consider about where Letterboxd is going. Related Stories Letterboxd Finalizing $330 Million Sale to The New York Times ‘The Weed Eaters’ Lands Expanded Release from Yellow Veil Pictures: New Zealand Cannibal Movie Sets Winter Rollout

There’s understandably a lot of negative social chatter about the news of Letterboxd’s looming acquisition, but let’s rest assured that it’s at least not a studio taking ownership of the wildly popular cinephile engagement platform. A24, Sony, Netflix, and Skydance were all reported to have registered talks about an acquisition. Whether or not this new iteration of Letterboxd will exist behind a paywall is one matter, but that’s not the worst thing compared to the potential studio-ification (i.e. A24-ification, as they were in talks for the sale) of the brand. Compare it to studios running an exhibition chain — not just Sony purchasing Alamo Drafthouse, but all the way back to the days before the Paramount Decrees, which legislatively blocked studios from having a monopoly on theaters. (Decrees that are no longer in effect.) In that situation, there’s more potential for marketing nepotism and favoritism to titles and properties in-house. A media company taking over Letterboxd should, in theory, prevent the kind of self-interest that threatens independence. —Ryan Lattanzio

A deal would bring two unusually loaded cultural conversations under one roof. The movie-logging platform has helped reshape the world’s repertory film scene — effectively gamifying the enjoyment of archival art — while debates about the Times often wind their way back to the paper’s coverage of Palestine and trans rights. For Letterboxd users who see that coverage as having real consequences for whose lives and experiences are taken seriously by mainstream journalistic institutions, the prospect of the Times owning a community they helped build raises questions of trust. A bigger audience would be a genuine upside, but for some users, who owns the room is an existential issue. —Alison Foreman

While some users might not even know about Letterboxd’s digital magazine, the Journal has been a growing presence on the platform, with a staffed editorial team regularly publishing interviews, retrospective considerations, film festival coverage, and other longform articles. The question remains on how, or if, those writers and editors will be integrated into the New York Times newsroom. A shuttering of the Journal would wreck yet another publication for professional film coverage and freelance opportunities, of which there are fewer and fewer. On the other hand, when the New York Times bought The Athletic in 2022 for a whopping $550 million, the banner initially continued as a semi-independent banner. But a year later, the Times dissolved its existing sports department, laying off or reassigning staff, and positioned The Athletic as a replacement. The New York Times’ culture desk has not been immune to shake-ups over recent years; the potential addition of Letterboxd begs the question of whether further changes are in store. —J. Kim Murphy

As the number of Letterboxd accounts has skyrocketed over the past few years, navigating the platform has become a bumpier experience for users. Pop-up Cloudflare turnstiles reading “Verifying you are human. This may take a few seconds” make frequent interruptions clicking from page to page, while Gremlins-centric error messages signaling server crashes are semi-regular occurrences. The New York Times draws much more web traffic than Letterboxd and such technical hiccups are essentially anomalous. The company certainly has the resources to bolster the strength of Letterboxd’s servers. —JKM

Letterboxd users have historically been an extremely discerning audience, sensitive to changes that might be seen as minute or inconsequential for other websites. A memorable hiccup from recent years came when the platform abruptly removed an option to list out all star-ratings given by the accounts one follows on a single web page. After some backlash from users (like myself) who noticed the feature’s disappearance, Letterboxd was swift in reintegrating the tool. It was a small crisis with a happy ending, but it speaks to how quickly UI changes can dishearten the platform’s users. If the New York Times wants to make even small tweaks to the platform, or heavily integrate it into its digital ecosystem, it will face an audience that’s quick to rally against such changes. —JKM

The New York Times Company is the poster child for brand elasticity in the digital media age. America’s newspaper of record didn’t just adapt to the Internet; it built an empire of games, recipes, and sports that a sizable chunk of the world needs to engage with in a daily basis. But it’s less apparent how Letterboxd fits into the strategy. The social network exists somewhere between an editorial product and a game and doesn’t have a clear comp within the NYT organization. Is the plan to simply move the entire Letterboxd infrastructure behind the NYT paywall, making the $30 monthly subscription tier even more unavoidable for cinephiles? Draw on users’ data to bolster revenue opportunities for streaming promotions and the Times’ product recommendation banner Wirecutter? The answer might be some combination of the above, but the Times is entering uncharted territory. —Christian Zilko

Plenty of filmmakers IndieWire has spoken to are concerned about the widening gap between what defines film criticism and what defines a hot-take social media sound-off, i.e., the “instant reaction.” Reviews on Letterboxd can range from the thoughtful and long-form to the pithy and snarky. As film critic jobs evaporate globally, what happens when you merge Letterboxd closer to the purview of established, institutional film writing, the kind that’s hard, that demands a chunk of your soul? Letterboxd has further democratized criticism, no question, and while many of us argue that we need an elevated discourse, what happens if more people start to think… we don’t? Will the fusion of the Times and Letterboxd stoke that debate, or create harmony? Will this only fuel the growing primacy of influencers over critics and journalists as an authority on a film’s quality? Either way, cantankerous conversation will abound. —RL

It follows then that if enough Letterboxd users distrust the Times, they might log fewer movies, post fewer reviews, or exit the app altogether. From a web-development perspective, the basic mechanics of a movie diary are incredibly easy to replicate. (Hell, AI just cloned Adobe Photoshop.) The hard part is getting the consumers whose aggregate taste is a cultural bellwether to once again show up in the same place. It wouldn’t take a mass exodus for Letterboxd to feel fundamentally different, and if the core group of people who reliably made consumers laugh or put weird repertory picks on your radar stop contributing, there will be fewer reasons to engage. The community could splinter across new competitor sites — which, yes, opens up potential opportunities for aspiring critics to gain exposure and find their followings. But we can’t know if any of that would be as big as the OG Letterboxd. —AF

#3534. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3533. Sony Officially Announces New Playstation Handheld

The PlayStation Portal is getting a Japan-only upgrade

While Sony has largely given up on the handheld market following the death of the now-lamented PlayStation Vita, the company is taking another swing at the PlayStation Portal. Following in Nintendo’s footsteps, Sony will release a Japan-only version of its handheld. The specs are mostly unchanged: the region-locked Portal will have the same 1080p LCD screen and will still be built around remotely accessing a PS5 to play games.

The big difference is that this version will have internal storage. Because of this added hard drive, the region-locked Portal will cost the same as the global model in Japan, 39,980 yen ($252). Like the Japan-exclusive PS5, it's in Midnight Black.

The PlayStation Portal's main selling point is that it lets users remotely stream games from their PS5 while connected to the same Wi-Fi as the console, so the base version doesn’t really need built-in storage. Adding a hard drive suggests the new version may eventually do more than stream; the product description says Sony included it “with an eye towards future functionality.” It’s unclear if that future functionality is for the PlayStation 5 or for the presumed PlayStation 6.

It isn’t surprising that Sony is releasing a Japan-only PlayStation Portal. The company previously took this approach with the PlayStation 5, releasing a region-locked version of the console for the equivalent of $350. Much like Nintendo released a Japan-only version of the Switch 2, Sony did this to make the system more accessible to domestic customers amid the yen’s declining purchasing power.

The PlayStation Portal sold reasonably well despite its seemingly limited use case, moving an estimated 420,000 units in the U.S. alone within its first year. However, critics had mixed reactions. While it was praised for its build and screen quality, many reviews found that even mild connection issues had a huge impact on gameplay. The system’s streaming-only design, combined with a $199.99 price point, made it a fairly niche device.

That said, Sony has improved the system's software over the years, adding better streaming settings for those with beefy home networks.

Perhaps the device's biggest change is that Sony eventually added cloud gaming support, meaning the device was no longer restricted to PS5 owners. This lets users play any game with PS Plus cloud support, as long as they have a PS Plus Premium subscription (which costs $159.99 a year). As hardware prices continue to rise due to an ongoing RAM shortage, console manufacturers may make another significant push for cloud gaming in the near future, with this revived PlayStation Portal being Sony's first major stab.

#3532. Before Euphoria, Sydney Sweeney Starred In An Overlooked Psychological Thriller That's Streaming For Free

2019 was a big year for Sydney Sweeney, marking her debut as Cassie Howard in HBO's "Euphoria." That proved to be her breakout role, but it wasn't her only memorable performance of 2019. That same year appeared in "Clementine" as Lana, a mysterious and beguiling figure who enters into a complicated relationship with another woman trying to reckon with a recently-ended love affair. Like Sweeney's character, the movie is hard to pin down. As Variety's Lisa Kennedy noted in her review, you're never quite sure whether this is "a coming-of-age meditation or a psychosexual thriller," a "breakup drama or simmering horror flick," making it a compelling watch throughout. All of which makes it a shame this one got lost in the shuffle — a result of having been overshadowed by Sweeney's "Euphoria" debut and the global pandemic of 2020. Thankfully, "Clementine" is now available to watch for free over on one of the best streaming services available, Tubi.

Sweeney hasn't always had the easiest time outside of "Euphoria." Thanks to the $100 million box office smash hit "Anyone But You" and her lead performance in Paul Feig's excellent, wicked drama "The Housemaid," the actor has managed to remain relevant. But Sweeney's 2025 film "Americana" was ignored at the box office and "Madame Web" speaks for itself.

That said, Sweeney has always subverted expectations and will no doubt continue to see success in the coming years. Heck, she has already overcome perceptions of her as an attractive young actor with little else to offer via excellent performances in a range of projects, many of which simply haven't been given the attention they deserve. "Clementine" is just one example.

/Film's list of the best Sydney Sweeney movies is a testament to the actor's versatility, with everything from romantic comedies to the intense, nerve wracking portrait of United States Air Force veteran Reality Winner that was "Reality." 2019's "Clementine" is harder to define but just as worthy of your attention.

The film is written and directed by Lara Jean Gallagher, and represents the Pennsylvania-native's debut narrative feature following a series of short films and commercials. It tells the story of 30-year-old Karen (Otmara Marrero), who, having broken up with her older girlfriend, D (Sonya Walger), travels to her ex's lake house to take stock of the relationship. There, she meets 19-year-old Lana (Sweeney), who's first seen sunbathing by the lake and very quickly captures Karen's attention. As the pair grow closer, Karen suddenly finds herself in a similar situation to D in her former relationship. Wary of developing feelings for someone significantly younger, yet hopelessly drawn to Lana, Karen has to navigate a delicate relationship.

Gallagher told Movablefest that with "Clementine" she wanted to interrogate the often contradictory nature of female relationships. "I was just really just interested in exploring female relationships," she said, "and how it can feel like a sister dynamic or like rivals, or like a mother/daughter at times or even sexual in nature all at the same time." That can be seen in the often confounding connection between Karen and Lana, which  makes for a movie that's at once tense and touching, hazy yet sharp.

Prior to her "Euphoria" debut, Sydney Sweeney was making a name for herself with roles in Netflix series "Everything Sucks!" and HBO's "Sharp Objects," in which she played a psychiatric patient Alice alongside Amy Adams' Camille Preaker. Sweeney also played Eden Spencer in Season 2 of "The Handmaid's Tale" and her star was clearly on the rise. It's a shame, then, that "Clementine" flew under the radar in the way that it did, as it boasts an enigmatic yet darkly enchanting performance from Sweeney that surely would have helped boost her profile had the film received more attention.

"Clementine" premiered at the 2019 Tribeca Film Festival ahead of distributor Oscilloscope Pictures releasing the film on virtual screens in May 2020 — a late pivot that came in the wake of the global pandemic. It managed a perfectly respectable 62% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, and while that may seem slightly underwhelming, certain critics were all in on Lara Gallagher's psychological thriller.

The aforementioned Lisa Kennedy praised Sweeney for "deftly shape-shift[ing] from late teen to younger — too young? — often within the same scene," while Slant's Jake Cole was convinced that Gallagher is "every bit as adept as Josephine Decker and the Safdie brothers are at wringing unease from the most mundane of scenarios." David Ehrlich of IndieWire might have felt the film was "too prone to navel-gazing to leave a strong impression" but Nell Minow of RogerEbert.com seemed to enjoy what she described as an "exploration of the shifting power in relationships with striking images and overtones of duality." So, if you're looking for a good psychological thriller, "Clementine" is arguably one of the best movies on Tubi right now.

#3531. Every Hercule Poirot Movie Actor, Ranked By Faithfulness To Agatha Christie's Books

Book to movie adaptations are one of the most longstanding traditions in Hollywood history. Ever since the very beginnings of the film industry, books have been adapted into movies by filmmakers eager to recreate the success of their literary counterparts on the big screen. This remains true even in 2026, with the most recent example being Verity, which proved, predictably, to be a big hit at the box office.

Verity is one of many Colleen Hoover novels to be made into films, and she’s not the first author to be the subject of several adaptations. There are, of course, the likes of J. K. Rowling (Harry Potter), Ian Fleming (James Bond), and Agatha Christie (Poirot, Miss Marple, etc.). The latter’s works in particular have been the subjects of countless adaptations; as of 2026, there have been over fifty official feature films made based off of Christie’s work, and that doesn’t include the many television series that have been made as well.

The majority of these Agatha Christie adaptations have come with the famous Belgian detective Hercule Poirot as the central protagonist. Poirot, a character first created for the novel The Mysterious Affair at Styles (written in 1916 and published in 1920), has had over a dozen film adaptations over the years. The first of these came with actor Austin Trevor playing the sleuth in two 1931 films, Alibi and Black Coffee.

Since then, nearly twenty actors have gone on to play Poirot. Some, like Trevor, have appeared in several films, while others have portrayed the character only once (and not always in a direct adaptation of Christie’s work, as is the case with Tom Petrone). Some of these actors are incredibly faithful to the novels; Peter Ustinov, for example, captured the essence of Poirot well. At the same time, some adaptations and actors have taken more liberties with the source material, opting for an original take (that hasn’t always come off).

Actor Tom Petrone played Hercule Poirot in just one film — 2008's Doing Agatha. Unlike many of the names on this list, Petrone isn’t starring as Poirot in a direct adaptation. Instead, Doing Agatha is a film that, as the title suggests, focuses on the author behind the character, rather than the character himself. Doing Agatha follows Christie as she navigates a chaotic production of her iconic play The Mousetrap.

Therefore, Petrone’s brief portrayal of Poirot is more of a meta take than a typical adaptation of the character. Yet, many of the classic Poirot elements are still present: he’s eccentric, confident, and exceptional at solving a mystery. However, at the same time, Poirot isn’t in this movie at great length, and the scenes he is in aren’t enough to flesh out his full character, making this the least faithful actor adaptation of the detective.

Hugh Laurie is arguably best known for playing Gregory House in the aptly titled medical drama series House. He’s also appeared in a number of beloved films and shows, including Sense and Sensibility, 101 Dalmatians, and Spice World. It’s the latter that gives Laurie the opportunity to play the iconic character of Hercule Poirot.

Spice World is, as the title suggests, a film that focuses on the British pop girl group the Spice Girls. All members of the group appeared in the film, which was inspired by The Beatles’ A Hard Day’s Night. One might be wondering, then, how Poirot comes into a story like this.

The answer is that Laurie appears in a dream sequence, and one in which he plays Poirot investigating a murder. In this scene, Baby Spice is there, holding a gun and ammunition, but Poirot doesn’t even begin to suspect her of murder (which is the film’s way of telling the audience that the Spice Girls could get away with anything).

In the books, Poirot is described as a chubby, short man, neither of which applies to Hugh Laurie. As a result, physically, Laurie isn’t the most faithful of adaptations. Additionally, his appearance as Poirot is used for comedic purposes only, so he doesn’t get a chance to show off the character’s classic personality or iconic traits. Yet, he does sport Poirot’s iconic mustache, which is something.

Another comedy film featuring Hercule Poirot is The Strange Case of the End of Civilization as We Know It, which debuted in 1977. The film, which was co-written by and stars John Cleese, is a comedic portrayal of Sherlock Holmes and his partner, Dr. John Watson. Once again, then, the question of how Poirot fits into a story like this, one centered on a completely different fictional detective, comes into play.

The answer is relatively simple, though. Cleese plays a heightened, ridiculous version of Holmes, and both of these traits also apply to the world that the film exists in. As a result, this opens the door for some creative liberties for the sake of comedy, with one sequence showing Holmes going to a party that is attended by a number of fictional detectives, including Poirot and Columbo.

Dudley Jones is the actor playing Poirot in this film, and once again, his screen time is limited. However, interestingly, Jones is able to capture many of the detective’s distinctive mannerisms, the same of which can’t be said about some of the other actors playing Poirot in a small role. That being said, this is yet again a relatively unfaithful adaptation, with the comedic tone being the core reason behind this.

James Coco doesn’t play Hercule Poirot by name, but he does play a character called Milo Perrier, who is a clear parody of the Christie’s detective, and, therefore, belongs on this list. Coco appears as Perrier, or Poirot, in 1976's Murder by Death, and captures the detective’s confidence (sometimes arrogance) well. However, Coco abandons many other elements of the character in service of the parody, making this another actor with an adaptation that takes plenty of liberties.

In 2004, the BBC released the film Agatha Christie: A Life in Pictures, which serves as a biography of sorts for the famous author. However, where there’s Christie, there’s usually Poirot, and that’s what happens in this adaptation. The film explores Christie’s infamous disappearance, and subsequent reappearance, which has been the subject of much speculation in the years since.

Interestingly, Welsh actor Anthony O’Donnell plays two characters in the made-for-television film: DCC William Kenward, the detective in charge of Christie’s disappearance, and Hercule Poirot himself. This allows Poirot, arguably Christie’s most famous creation, to be a part of her real life story, even if he himself is fictional.

O’Donnell captures the general essence of the character well, for which he deserves great credit. That being said, this is a story firmly centered on Agatha Christie, so he doesn’t get much of a chance to shine.

One of the most famous actors on this list, Ian Holm played Hercule Poirot briefly in Murder by the Book in 1986. This is another film that focuses on Agatha Christie herself rather than the fictional characters she created, but Poirot does find a way to sneak into the story.

Despite a relatively brief appearance, Holm portrays a memorable version of Poirot, leading many to wish that he would have had another opportunity to play the character in his career. Holm brings a sizable screen presence to his Poirot, and has the intelligence and charm so strongly associated with the character.

An earlier adaptation of Christie’s work is The Alphabet Murders, which released in 1965. Tony Randall plays Poirot in this film, but the script takes considerable liberties with the detective. For one, many of his quirks, like his confidence, accent, and appearance, are often played for laughs, which Christie’s books never do. Yet, Randall does play Poirot with an exceptional amount of eccentricity, which is exactly what’s needed to bring a character like this to life.

The aforementioned Austin Trevor was the very first actor to play Hercule Poirot on screen, taking on the role in three films: Alibi (1931), Black Coffee (1931) and Lord Edgware Dies (1934). Trevor deserves praise for his performance, which helped to establish Poirot as a character made for the big screen, even if there are many changes from the book.

Trevor lacks the traditional appearance of Poirot, for example, as he’s a relatively tall and skinny man. At the same time, this version also lacks Poirot’s famous mustache, which makes him feel considerably less like the character from the books.

Alfred Molina took on the role of Poirot in the television film adaptation of Murder on the Orient Express in 2001. Molina’s adaptation is much more faithful than Trevor’s, however, as the actor has the traditional appearance of Poirot, equipped with an instantly recognizable mustache. Molina also captures Poirot’s intelligence incredibly well, showing him to be a very capable detective, but this is undercut by the changes made to the story as a whole, as the film is set in the modern day, as opposed to the early 20th century.

Kenneth Branagh was the last actor to play Poirot on the big screen, and he did so in three films: Murder on the Orient Express, Death on the Nile, and A Haunting in Venice. The first two are relatively straightforward adaptions of the books, but the third takes more creative liberties. Yet, throughout all three, Branagh’s portrayal of the character remains largely faithful to the source material.

This version of Poirot is arrogant, intelligent, and has all the idiosyncratic qualities that the character normally has (and he even has a comically large mustache as well). The only major change that Branagh makes is that his version of Poirot is relatively tall and lean, going against the stockier build that the detective is known for in the novels.

#3530. Eric Bauza’s Final ‘Looney Tunes’ Performance Is ‘Daffy Season,’ Now in Theaters Ahead of ‘The Cat in the Hat’

The death of Eric Bauza in October shocked the entertainment industry. An impressively prolific voice actor, it would’ve been nearly impossible for anybody engaging with animation over the past 15 years to never come across his work. Bauza’s death came just two months after the delayed release of “Coyote vs. Acme,” the “Looney Tunes” feature once deemed unreleasable by Warner Bros. Discovery and later sold off to Ketchup Entertainment. The film, which grossed $101 million worldwide, is a true showcase for Bauza, who lends his voice to a plethora of iconic characters, including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Tweety, and Porky Pig. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Thunders with $31.6 Million, Scoring the Biggest Debut Ever for a Live-Action, Foreign Language Film Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Roars with $6.7 Million in Previews, ‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’ Earns $3.5 Million

Bauza became something of the defining voice of modern “Looney Tunes” in his final years. Fans can see him give one final performance with the property in “Daffy Season,” a 7-minute animated short that plays before screenings of “The Cat in the Hat,” opening Friday from Skydance’s Warner Bros. Pictures. A representative for the studio confirmed to IndieWire that the short is Bauza’s final “Looney Tunes” movie. Bauza is also credited as providing additional voices for “The Cat in the Hat.”

“Daffy Season” centers on Daffy Duck, voiced by Bauza. He’s joined by Jeff Bergman as Bugs Bunny, Gabriel Iglesias as Speedy Gonzales, and Jeannie Tirado as Lola Bunny. The plot follows Daffy, turning his beak up at his fellow Tunes as they mindlessly obsess over the game of soccer. Todd Wilderman and Hamish Grieve are co-directors. “Daffy Season” is the first theatrically released “Looney Tunes” short since “Daffy’s Rhapsody” played before “Journey 2: The Mysterious Island” back in 2012.

Before “Daffy Season,” Bauza had already provided some voice work for a “Tunes” musical feature titled “Bye Bye Bunny,” which was canceled after some years of development and production. Other “Looney Tunes” credits from Bauza include the HBO Max series “Looney Tunes Cartoons” and the features “The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie” and “Space Jam: A New Legacy.”

Bauza died at his home in Los Angeles on October 25 as a result of hypertensive cardiovascular disease. A group of organizers have launched a GoFundMe campaign to gather financial support for his son, Ryker Bauza, and Ryker’s mother, Jessica Borutski.

In a tribute in The Hollywood Reporter, Warner Bros. Pictures Animation producer Susan Rogers credited Bauza with playing a huge role in reviving the “Looney Tunes.”

“There wasn’t a single short he couldn’t quote or couldn’t reference,” she said. “I don’t think you replace Eric Bauza … The hole he leaves is huge. There are many talented people out there, and the franchise will move on. But there’s only one Eric Bauza.”

#3529. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

#3528. Dylan Skolnick Returning as Co-Director of the Cinema Arts Centre Following Protests and Boycotts

Dylan Skolnick is returning as Director of the Cinema Arts Centre following protests and boycotts over his firing.

In a post announcing Skolnick’s reinstatement, the Long Island cultural institution said that its board of directors had sat down for a series of meetings with an independent mediator. “Those discussions have resulted in an agreement to move forward together, and we are pleased to welcome Dylan back to the Cinema,” the announcement read.

In September, Skolnick was ousted by the CAC board of directors for “serious misconduct.” In justifying the move, the organization slammed Skolnick as a “dysfunctional” and “disloyal” manager whose freelance work as a film buyer for other indie cinemas was a conflict of interest. Skolnick and his supporters countered that the CAC board was experiencing a “hostile takeover” and said that his moonlighting as a film buyer was common practice in the business. Skolnick said he had informed an earlier iteration of the board of his work, but conceded that the current leadership was unaware of his side gig. Related Stories ‘You Can See Everything’ Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release

Skolnick had deep ties to the institution, which his parents had founded in Huntington, New York more than 50 years ago, as well as strong connections to the wider filmmaking world. Major figures such as Edie Falco, Kent Jones, and Isabella Rossellini leapt to his support, while donations to the CAC dried up, and box office receipts cratered, IndieWire reported last month.

The CAC said that as part of Skolnick’s reinstatement, a new co-director will be hired in the coming months to help lead the organization and its board will invite several new members, “including individuals with backgrounds and experience in the film world.” Skolnick and his fellow co-director and and the CAC board will “undergo additional training focused on effective governance, leadership, accountability and fostering a positive workplace culture.”

In a statement, the CAC leadership acknowledged the fissures created by Skolnick’s ouster, as well as the need to repair relationships and address the non-profit’s financial challenges.

“We want to extend our deepest gratitude to everyone who spoke up, showed their support, and stood by the Cinema during one of the most challenging periods in its history,” the theater said in a statement. “Your voices made a difference, and your continued commitment to this institution means more than we can express.”

#3526. 'It Gets Worse' Puts a Brutally Honest Gen Z Spin on 'Girls' With Mixed Results | Review

Greer Riddell is a London-based film and television journalist writing about comedy, streaming and the evolving media industry in the UK and USA. She works at Collider, covering the latest in film, television and entertainment through interviews, features, reviews and industry coverage.

Her recent brand collaborations include HBO, Warner Bros., Netflix, Hulu, Sky, Disney+ and DC Studios. She has covered titles including Saturday Night Live UK, Rivals, Scrubs, Stuart Fails to Save the Universe, Ludwig, Supergirl and Stranger Things.

Her recent interviews include Florence Pugh, Mike Faist and Christopher Abbott for Netflix's East of Eden, Taika Waititi and Jenna Ortega for Klara and the Sun.

It’s the Gen Z version of Lena Dunham’s Girls, but with even less optimism and considerably more hook-ups. It Gets Worse is a sex-fueled sitcom with sharp writing and a strong set of characters you’ll find yourself more disgusted with than sympathetic toward. It captures the messiness, self-awareness and general hopelessness of being young in the modern world, and you'll feel glad you’re no longer in your twenties.

Written by and starring Leo Reich as Ethan, the series is a British-Canadian collaboration produced by A24 for Channel 4 and Crave. It’s been a year since Ethan, Abi (Emily Fairn) and Sam (Olive Gray) moved to London, and now their landlord is asking them to leave their first house share. With a new contract looming, the three friends must find somewhere else to live, but their housing arrangements soon become the least of their problems. They drift apart, fall into toxic relationships and increasingly questionable situations before eventually moving back in together. All three are beginning to question whether the humiliation they are living through will eventually get better. As the title suggests, it doesn't.

When Girls first aired on HBO in 2012, Dunham was hailed as the main millennial commentator, with her series frequently praised for its accurate depiction of young women navigating adulthood. Now, her involvement in It Gets Worse feels like a passing of the baton, mentoring the next generation as they create a series that is truly their own commentary. But Reich's project is a far cry from the optimism of the generation that came before; this is Gen Z's turn, and their outlook is considerably bleaker.

On the surface, It Gets Worse is about the difficulty of making friends as a young adult, particularly when those friendships are often built around little more than sex, partying and whoever happens to live closest to your dingy London flat. It captures the reality of moving to the capital away from your family, where the jobs, money and social life are supposedly waiting rather than settling for the get-married-to-your-high-school-boyfriend life. But Reich's series is interested in the downside of that supposed freedom. There is an emptiness to life on the other side of university, when the bubble of youth has burst, and you find yourself at the mercy of situations and people rather than feeling in control of your own future. Ethan, Abi, and Sam's storylines are permeated by depression and Gen Z's seemingly genetic sense of dread, as they struggle to recognize their own worth or understand what might actually make them happy. The series is essentially waiting for them to realize that they are the ones in control of their futures, rather than continuing to let other people and circumstances dictate their every move.

Reich's scripts are wonderfully wry, rarely straying away from the controversial and relishing the opportunity to shock the audience. Yet their cynicism feels entirely in keeping with the way Gen Z communicates. It is self-aware, picking up on generational stereotypes and narratives and amplifying them for a laugh, while simultaneously making you feel sorry for the people at the center of them. It Gets Worse has Gen Z's anti-perfectionist, messy and occasionally gross vibe down to a T. It’s littered with references to MUBI, Monzo, Hinge, ChatGPT, negroni sbagliatos and turmeric shots. There’s even a cameo from Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg as Emily, a woman who was engaged to overseas royalty and owned a Tesla — the defining signal of success.

One of the more unusual elements of It Gets Worse is its narrator, novelist Zadie Smith, who reads the poetic yet abstract writings of Gray's Sam throughout. You’re initially encouraged to keep up with the metaphors and abstractions, hoping that somewhere within them lies a poignant emotional explanation for why these friends behave the way they do. However, they gradually fade into obscurity when you realize they aren't necessarily providing one. Ethan later confirms that details included in Sam's writing aren't factual in any way, just put together in an attempt to reconcile their friendship in the finale.

Throughout the series, the three friends have drifted away from the personalities that made them click in the first place. It Gets Worse posits that the people you were at university, when you first met and became friends, were perhaps the real versions of yourselves. The world outside that youthful bubble, along with its responsibilities and fears, has changed you, and perhaps the answer is to find your way back to those earlier selves. It is a rather romantic notion, but one that deserves some scrutiny. While there is certainly something to be said for remaining true to yourself, your university self is also your younger, more naive self, and that’s clear from the situations Ethan, Abi and Sam find themselves in. Growing up inevitably changes people, and It Gets Worse is at its most interesting when it acknowledges how difficult it is to work out which parts of yourself you should leave behind and which are worth holding on to.

The series also loves to make its audience uncomfortable. It accurately shows the horror of being a young adult making questionable decisions, but knowing we’ve all gone through that stage doesn't always make for an easy or particularly amusing watch. Andrew Scott, best known for playing Fleabag's hot priest, begins the series as Brian, Ethan's therapist, who he subsequently hooks up with. The relationship isn't established before the dirty talk begins, making the encounter all the more shocking when Brian reduces Ethan to being a "hole for daddy." Similarly, Sam tutors a young boy preparing for his GCSE exams, only for it to emerge that he has a crush on her. He even follows her to a spoken-word night, where she has just spent time slating him on stage for being an incel. Some of the sexual encounters are genuinely difficult to watch, not necessarily because they are explicit but because of how emotionally toxic they are. It Gets Worse doesn't shy away from the fact that the horror of being in your twenties often comes from the decisions you make yourself.

While Reich's Ethan is the most charismatic of the three leads, Fairn's Abi is arguably the most outwardly relatable. She is keen to settle down with whichever man can offer her the sort of life she can upload onto Instagram, ideally making residual school acquaintances think better of her in the process. Without really considering who or what would make her happy, she settles for Tom (Sean Delaney), who is just about every thirty-something heterosexual man in London rolled into one. He goes bouldering, idolizes Anthony Bourdain and cooks various cuts of meat using TikTok tutorials while mansplaining the entire process. While Ethan endures disastrous hook-ups, vomits on himself and eventually has to move back in with his Mum in Edgware (heaven forbid), Abi is busy pursuing the suburban “dream.” It Gets Worse understands that, for a 24-year-old, one of the greatest failures in life is settling down. Abi also works in HR, if things weren't already bleak enough.

That is perhaps the series' genius. Reich has a laser-focused grasp on character and voice. From the three leads to supporting roles such as Louise (Emmeline Downie), every person feels like a personality you would actually encounter in real life. You immediately understand what type of person they are and what Reich is trying to say about them, often through the way they talk rather than what they actually say. It is a particularly impressive knack for characterization, and one that gives the series its sharpest comedic moments. One standout involves Abi discovering Tom's silicone sex toy and confronting him about it over the dinner he has just prepared for her and her friends. There are also situations where, if you're outside the Gen Z bracket, you might struggle to believe they actually happen, like a warehouse sex party that is filmed and subsequently screened as a tragic art project. It is the sort of storyline that makes you question whether Reich is exaggerating for comic effect or simply documenting a generation that has become accustomed to turning every personal humiliation into content.

Ethan's relationship with his mother (Vicki Pepperdine) is another highlight. Their dynamic is amusing to watch, particularly as the lines she delivers, such as "keep the noise down, your voice travels", feel so authentic that you could easily believe the two are a real mother and son. It is also fun to see Blake Harrison, of The Inbetweeners fame, playing another gormless character, this time Roger, Ethan's mother's lodger, who also happens to have a crush on her.

It Gets Worse will appeal to plenty of Gen Z viewers, who will marvel at Reich's ability to put people who sound and act exactly like their friends on screen. There are countless quips and lines to enjoy in the script, and its understanding of generational attitudes is impressively sharp. Yet it also drags you down into the dank depression of being back in your twenties, trying to survive independently for the first time, surrounded by questionable friends and without a clear point of view. It is a series that knows exactly how to make its audience laugh, but it also wants you to recognize the uncomfortable reality behind the comedy. The freedom of moving to London, making new friends and building a life for yourself can quickly become an exhausting cycle of flat-sharing, disastrous relationships and trying to convince yourself that everything is going to plan. Ethan, Abi and Sam may be surrounded by opportunity, but none of them seem particularly equipped to make the most of it.

Reich has created a sitcom that is unapologetically Gen Z, complete with the generation's distinct vocabulary, cultural references, self-awareness, and seemingly endless capacity for humiliation. Its strong set of characters are brought to life by an even stronger script, although its relentless cynicism and emotionally uncomfortable scenarios can make it a rather draining watch. It Gets Worse may be an accurate reflection of what it feels like to be young and directionless today, but it is also a reminder of just how miserable that experience can be.

It Gets Worse premiered November 6 on Paramount+.

A candid Gen Z sitcom about messy realities and harsh truths.

#3525. 6 Best Bryan Cranston TV Shows (That Aren't Breaking Bad)

Breaking Bad is the kind of success that overshadows all the other successes that one might have. George Lucas has forever been associated with Star Wars; Phoebe Waller-Bridge will forever be associated with Fleabag. Bryan Cranston was already one of TV’s most iconic actors long before he turned Mr. Chips into Scarface, thanks to his sitcom roles in Seinfeld and Malcolm in the Middle, and since Breaking Bad, he’s been in both dark dramas like Your Honor and lighter comedies like The Studio.

But Breaking Bad isn’t just Cranston’s most acclaimed work; it’s not hyperbole to say it might be the finest TV series ever created (although The Sopranos, The Wire, Six Feet Under, and its own spinoff Better Call Saul would all like a word). Nearly two decades later, Breaking Bad still regularly tops lists of the greatest TV shows of all time, and we continue to see its influence in shows like Barry and Narcos and Your Friends and Neighbors.

Walter White will always be Cranston’s greatest role — it brought together Cranston’s comedic and dramatic abilities, and allowed him to chart a character’s gradual transformation over the course of 63 episodes — and, by extension, Breaking Bad will always be his crowning professional achievement. But Cranston has starred in a bunch of great TV shows that weren’t Breaking Bad, and they deserve their due flowers; they deserve their moment in the sun, away from the shade of Heisenberg’s formidable shadow.

After a monstrous success like Breaking Bad, there’s a lot of pressure on what the key creatives do next. When Matt Groening created his second series after The Simpsons, it had a lot to live up to (and Futurama lived up to it). Cranston’s immediate follow-up to Breaking Bad was a show called Sneaky Pete. Cranston isn’t the star — that would be Giovanni Ribisi; Cranston is just a supporting player — but Cranston was heavily involved behind the scenes: he co-created the series with House’s David Shore and even has a story credit on the pilot.

Ribisi plays a con man who assumes the identity of his prison cellmate to evade a ruthless gangster, played by Cranston. Cranston only ever acted in the first season of Sneaky Pete, but the whole thing was a delightfully pulpy crime caper. It shared some of Breaking Bad’s dark humor, but it was less overtly comedic and more focused on the gritty thrills.

After playing a recurring role in Sneaky Pete and a handful of guest roles elsewhere, Cranston’s first starring role in a drama series post-Breaking Bad was in Showtime’s two-season gem Your Honor. Much like in Breaking Bad, Cranston plays a seemingly good man whose morals are tested when he’s unexpectedly thrust into extreme circumstances. In this case, Cranston plays a distinguished New Orleans judge whose teenage son accidentally kills the teenage son of a mob boss.

The story is all about how far you would go for your kids, in either direction. Cranston’s judge abandons his long-standing lawfulness to help his son out of a criminal jam, while the mob boss will stop at nothing to avenge his late offspring. Your Honor is nowhere near as riveting or complex as Breaking Bad, but it satisfies purely as a ripping yarn (and, of course, Cranston never disappoints).

From the moment Better Call Saul premiered, there was speculation about how and when and why Walter White would show up in the spinoff. In the end, Walt didn’t reappear until the back end of the final season, because there was no reason for him to appear any earlier in this prequel timeline. Better Call Saul went back to show us why Saul decided to represent Walt in the first place, what happened in the RV after that initial confrontation in the desert, and gave us an extra scene of Walt and Saul hiding out at the vacuum store.

Much like he did in the movie spinoff El Camino, Cranston slipped effortlessly back into the role of Walt. That scene in the basement, in particular, highlighted all of Walt’s worst qualities, namely his arrogance, his temper, and his impatience for the less intelligent. Better Call Saul is a rare spinoff that may have actually surpassed the original. By the end, the spinoff had become so gripping that it didn’t even need Walt (but it was nice to see him again, nonetheless).

Long before Breaking Bad, long before Malcolm in the Middle, the first show to put Bryan Cranston on the map was Seinfeld. Cranston played the recurring role of Tim Whatley, a dentist who started out as a love interest for Elaine, but quickly became something else entirely.

Whatley turned his dental office into an anything-goes sexual bazaar; he accused Jerry of being an “anti-dentite” with a prejudice against dentists. Whenever Cranston showed up in Seinfeld, you knew it was going to be a funny episode. Whatley is responsible for “regifting,” one of the greatest and most universally applicable Seinfeldisms.

When Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg realized that Hollywood is more absurd than ever, and yet there hasn’t been a really great Hollywood satire in at least a decade (arguably not since Tropic Thunder), they set out to make it themselves. With a fast-moving Larry Sanders vérité style, The Studio has encapsulated the ridiculousness of the modern movie business, with storylines involving soulless sequels, generative A.I., and the plundering of useless I.P. like Kool-Aid and Minecraft.

Cranston popped up in the first and last episodes of The Studio to steal the show. He plays Griffin Mill, the CEO of Continental Studios, who promotes Rogen’s Matt Remick to replace Catherine O’Hara’s Patty as the head of the studio in the pilot. After setting up all that exposition in the series premiere, Cranston got to have a lot more fun when he returned for the two-part finale. After unwittingly ingesting several pounds of magic mushrooms, Griffin collapses into a drug-induced spiral, and all his underlings have to get him on his feet for the big CinemaCon presentation that will save the company in just a few hours.

In those last couple of episodes, Cranston really throws himself into the physicality of a mushroom trip. It’s a physical comic performance on par with Charlie Chaplin or Buster Keaton or Jackie Chan, and I don’t make that comparison lightly.

Even before he’d played Walter White in Breaking Bad, Bryan Cranston could’ve retired a TV legend, because he’d already played Hal in Malcolm in the Middle. In all the ways that Cranston’s turn as Walt is one of the finest dramatic performances in television history, his turn as Hal is one of the finest comedic performances. Hal is the ultimate portrait of the doofy, dorky dad; everyone could see their own father in that character. From the roller-skating episode to the speed-walking episode, Cranston always committed 100% to the absurdity and physicality of whatever comic scenario the Malcolm writers threw at him.

Breaking Bad obviously hits on a much deeper emotional level than Malcolm in the Middle, but relatable, sweet-natured comedy like this has its place, too. (Having said that, Malcolm wasn’t totally family-friendly; it was basically a punk-rock sitcom, with a lot of pitch-black humor.) Where most Hollywood depictions of family life enjoy white-collar wealth, Malcolm in the Middle accurately reflected a working-class existence where both parents have full-time jobs and all three kids share a bedroom.

#3523. Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Thunders with $31.6 Million, Scoring the Biggest Debut Ever for a Live-Action, Foreign Language Film

The year of unlikely box office smashes continues as “Godzilla Minus Zero” opened to a thunderous $31.6 million, shattering records to become the biggest North American debut for a live-action foreign language film in history. It easily toppled the previous benchmark established in 2002 by the wuxia epic “Hero,” which kicked off with $17.8 million. Globally, “Godzilla Minus Zero’s” haul stands at $63 million.

And it comes on the heels of a string of films that have defied conventional wisdom to resonate with moviegoers. Yes, the box office is still dominated by sequels and comic book movies like “Toy Story 5” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” but there’s been a lot more variety. Audiences have turned out in force for an original sci-fi adventure (“Project Hail Mary,” $684.6 million worldwide); a pair of low-budget horror films from 20-something auteurs with YouTube pedigree (“Obsession,” $524.3 million worldwide; “Backrooms,” $400.6 million worldwide); an adaptation of a Greek epic we were all forced to read in school (“The Odyssey,” $1.8 billion worldwide), and a three-hour documentary about a Silicon Valley cheat (“You Can See Everything,” $73.7 million and counting). Clearly, people are looking for something different. Related Stories ‘You Can See Everything’ Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release

In the case of “Godzilla Minus Zero,” it helped that the first film, 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One,” was an unexpected sleeper hit, grossing an impressive $57.1 million. But the first “Godzilla” opened to a mere $11.4 million, showing that the audience for the first monster movie grew on home entertainment. “Godzilla Minus Zero” is poised to bypass its predecessor to become the highest-grossing live-action Japanese movie in history. Once again, the film was directed by Takashi Yamazaki, who also worked on the special effects, produced by Japan’s Tojo, and distributed in the U.S. by GKids.

The success of “Godzilla Minus Zero” also demonstrates that subtitles are no barrier to box office success, something that Netflix and other streamers discovered with the popularity of local-language programming like “Squid Game,” “Money Heist,” and “Lupin.” The story at multiplexes is no different. U.S. audiences have filled auditoriums to watch “Parasite” ($53.8 million domestic), “Ne Zha 2” ($23.2 million domestic), and “Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba – The Movie: Infinity Castle” ($136.9 million domestic). The outsized grosses for “Godzilla Minus Zero” probably mean we haven’t heard the last of the fire-breathing Kaiju.

The monster movie made quick work of its main competition, Warner Bros. Animation’s “The Cat in the Hat,” which stumbled with $20 million domestically and $30 million globally. The family film cost $92 million to produce and extends a string of misses for Warner Bros., which was recently purchased by Skydance. Insiders say that the studio has lost hundreds of millions of dollars on bombs like “Digger,” “Supergirl,” and “The Bride!” and “The Cat in the Hat” won’t do much to mop up all that red ink.

#3522. The Google Pixel Watch 5 Is $100 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has knocked $100 off the latest Google Pixel Watch 5 (45mm, LTE), bringing it down to $429.99 from $529.99, its lowest price yet, according to price trackers. If you can do without cellular connectivity, the 45mm wifi model is also down by $100, now selling for a record-low $329.99 (down from $429.99). Plus, either one comes with 90 days of free Amazon Music. PCMag calls the Pixel Watch 5 the best smartwatch for Android users, largely because Gemini is built in so deeply—the assistant works proactively, so it can surface your flight details on the way to the airport or suggest a contact's number while you text about dinner plans, and a new AI-powered Health Coach reviews your workouts with tailored feedback, though some of its fitness advice sits behind a paid subscription.

Helping all of those AI features along is a faster Qualcomm processor that Google says improves the overall performance of this smartwatch by 20%, while RAM increases from 2GB to 3GB and storage doubles to 64GB compared with the Pixel Watch 4. As for its health hardware, Google left it largely untouched, so you still get heart rate and blood oxygen monitoring, ECG readings, skin temperature, GPS, and sleep tracking, with reportedly accurate findings. The catch is that this remains an Android-only watch, requiring Android 12 or newer, and some of the better AI features work best with a newer Pixel phone.

Physically, the Watch 5 doesn’t stray far from its predecessor, keeping the familiar domed display under 3D Corning Gorilla Glass while adding new watch faces that curve around its edges—with the screen reaching up to 3,000 nits and adjusting to ambient light, so it should remain easy to read during a sunny afternoon run or in a dim room.
