#3381. Farewell to Richard Lloyd, the Wild Guitar Boy at the Heart of Television

The music world is in mourning Richard Lloyd, the guitar virtuoso from Television, the New York band that put CBGB on the map and kicked off the punk rock explosion. Lloyd made Television one of the all-time great guitar bands, in his tumultuous partnership with Tom Verlaine. He died on Saturday, at 75, after a fight with cancer. But he created a lifetime’s worth of rock magic with Television, in classics like “Marquee Moon,” “Little Johnny Jewel,” and “Days.”

Television barely stuck together for five years and two albums — yet that was enough to change how guitar music has sounded ever since. They never got a shot at American radio airplay, but they inspired upstarts all over the world, like R.E.M., U2, Sonic Youth, and Radiohead. Lloyd played so many of their most dazzling solos, as in “Elevation,” “Guiding Light,” or “See No Evil,” where his guitar sums up all the “destructive urges” Verlaine sings about. You could devote your whole life to exploring Television live bootlegs, and some of us do.

Lloyd was always underrated — the George Harrison figure in Television, a couple of years younger than Verlaine, but constantly rebelling against his kid-brother status. He was the band’s wild child, the chaotic rock & roll hellion with the face of a choirboy. Verlaine didn’t touch drugs; Lloyd gobbled them up. Verlaine hated bars and clubs; Lloyd hated leaving. As he recalled in his memoir, “I called myself a try-sexual at the time, because I would try anything a couple of times to see if I liked it. For a while, I supported myself as a male prostitute, just like Dee Dee Ramone, around the corner of 53rd and 3rd.”

Television weren’t built to last — not with these volatile personalities. “I’m already a manic depressive – bipolar A, as they say,” Lloyd told Guitar World earlier this year. “Every time we went into the studio, Tom would literally drive me nuts. He would act in such a way that I would end up in the mental hospital, or just the regular hospital.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

But nobody — except maybe Verlaine — could miss the spectral beauty of their twin-guitar chemistry. Together, they made the timeless 1977 classic Marquee Moon. With Lloyd on Strat and Verlaine on Jazzmaster, they plugged into the urban grime of New York City and came up with a whole new kind of psychedelic punk. Lloyd was Bob Weir to Verlaine’s Jerry Garcia, Phife Dawg to his Q-Tip, Carl Wilson to his Brian, with the tough rhythm section of Fred Smith and Billy Ficca giving both axemen room to stretch out. Smith died this past February, Verlaine in 2023, leaving Ficca as the last man standing.

Lloyd was a New York kid who grew up in Greenwich Village, at the height of the Sixties party. By all accounts, he jumped right in, prowling the city for sex and drugs and adventure. He also faced mental health issues, getting locked up in various institutions, given chemical shock treatment.

But Lloyd had a superhuman knack for charming people, with his magnetic looks and personality, talking his way into any room. As he recalled, “I was a vagabond, but a pretty one.” He hit the Fillmore East to see the Grateful Dead or Led Zeppelin or the Allman Brothers, the kind of guy who could always get in free. He was brazen enough to walk in on a Dead soundcheck and ask Jerry Garcia to put him on the guest list that night. As Lloyd told the tale, Phil Lesh was the one who said yes.

He was always a wild thing. In his highly entertaining 2018 memoir Everything Is Combustible, he recalls an incident from his teen years, when he was in Central Park but suddenly decided he wanted to move to another planet. So he walked all the way to the World Trade Center, 120 blocks or so—barefoot. As he wrote, “I found elevators that eventually took me up to the 106th floor. I entered an office and asked where the World Trade Center was. That is, where was the trading center where I could change worlds?” Related Content Richard Lloyd, Television's Virtuoso Guitarist, Dead at 75 Television Guitarist Richard Lloyd Diagnosed With Bile-Duct Cancer Watch the First Teaser for ‘Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story’ Melissa Gilbert Urges Stage Parents to ‘Be Sure’ It’s What Child Wants in Wake of Daveigh Chase Death

The question didn’t go over well. “As I found out, they also had jail cells on the 103rd floor, one of which they put me in.” They took him to Bellevue — not his first mental ward, and not his last.

He rambled from Boston to L.A., returning to NYC in 1973 with platinum-blonde hair, to catch his new favorite band, the glam-punk pioneers in the New York Dolls. He knew how to slither into any scene, immediately making himself the prettiest kid there. He became a regular at Max’s Kansas City, scamming the free chicken wings and finding lovesick older men to offer him places to stay. One of these men was Terry Ork, an Andy Warhol cohort who managed the bookstore Cinemabilia, where the employees included future punk legends Tom Verlaine, Richard Hell, and Robert Quine.

One night, Ork took him to an open-mic night to see Verlaine play solo. As soon as he sang “Venus,” Lloyd knew they belonged in a band together. Verlaine had already formed the Neon Boys with his high-school friend and fellow poet Richard Hell, but Lloyd was the real neon boy that they were looking for, the flashy brat, the agent of chaos in a band full of uptight control freaks. Lloyd made them a real rock & roll band instead of an art project.

Television found a place to play in March 1974 — a sleazy Bowery dive bar called CBGB. “Tom and I were walking down from his house to the loft in Chinatown,” Lloyd recalled in Clinton Heylin’s essential punk history From the Velvets to the Voidoids, “and we passed this place which the owner was outside fixing up. We asked if maybe we could play there—and he told us he was going to call the place Country, Bluegrass, and Blues. So we said, ‘Yes, we play stuff like that.’”

A ridiculous claim — but somehow, people always seemed eager to believe anything Richard Lloyd told them. Hilly Kristal called their bluff, and suddenly Television had a weekly residency. They played CBGB every Sunday night, drawing 20 or 30 people, until word began to spread. David Bowie came by in May, and declared them “the most original band I’ve seen in New York. They have it.” They drew stars like Lou Reed, Paul Simon, and director Nick Ray, who called them “four cats with a passion.” The NYC punk scene blew up at CBGB, with rebels like the Ramones, Patti Smith, Blondie, and Talking Heads. As Lloyd boasted in 2007, “CBGBs is the most famous rock & roll club to have ever existed and I fucking created it!”

Patti Smith put Television on the map with her famous Rock Scene review in 1974, before the band even had a record out. “Richard Lloyd plays emotional and highly sexually aware guitar,” she wrote. “He’s the pouty boyish one. The one most likely to get beat up in a parking lot.” Smith totally nailed the mystique of the band as “a movement of inspired mutants that will take the slop out of rock.”

But Tom Verlaine and Richard Hell battled for control of the band, until Hell quit and Fred Smith took over on bass. His chops let Television develop into the jam-till-dawn groove monsters they were born to be, stretching out into double-digit minutes for twin-guitar epics like “Marquee Moon” and “Friction.” They cut their debut indie single in 1975, with a tame studio version of “Little Johnny Jewel,” barely hinting at its onstage power. Lloyd hated it so much he quit for three days.

Television made two great 1970s studio albums: Marquee Moon is the universally acclaimed classic, while Adventure is the wrongly underrated follow-up. (As the zine guru Byron Coley once wrote, “Marquee Moon for songs, Adventure for playing.”) Instead of splitting into conventional lead/rhythm roles, they traded off solos. (Verlaine, prickly as always, made sure the album credits itemized which ones he played.) Lloyd brought the melodic sparkle of their succinct pop tunes, like “Venus” and “Days.” But he also brought the urgent rhythmic drive — Verlaine always needed a guitar partner to give his music a kick in the ass, and he never had one who kicked like Lloyd. You can hear that in fiery live documents like The Blow Up, with their famous destruction of Bob Dylan’s “Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door.”

There’s nothing like the magic these guys conjured up onstage. To hear Richard Lloyd at his best, go to the summer of 1978, when they already knew they were breaking up, but playing the most ferocious guitar fireworks of their lives. Check out the 12-minute “Little Johnny Jewel” from the San Francisco gig, finally released as Live at the Old Waldorf — a blowout that feels like a defiant last stand. Or the 17-minute “Marquee Moon” from Portland, a few nights later. Or the 13-minute “Kingdom Come” from back in NYC on July 29. It’s downright bizarre that so much of their greatest work remains officially unreleased.

But in any version, “Marquee Moon” is their zenith, the mutant love-child of “Dark Star” and “Sister Ray,” an epic trip into the unknown that wandered somewhere different every night. Lloyd delivered the garage-band propulsion, while Verlaine aimed for the interstellar jazz space of John Coltrane or Albert Ayler. “Marquee Moon” has been covered by bands from Pavement to Geese to Wilco — none of them trying to match the original, just to live up to that adventurous spirit.

Television never sold diddly in the U.S., but they made a worldwide splash. “Marquee Moon” became an unlikely hit single in the U.K, making the Top 30, while they also made the charts with “Prove It” and “Foxhole.” Adventure was a Top Ten album there, proving this band had a bright Eighties future. But sadly, Television were already falling apart, and so was Lloyd — a “full-blown junkie,” by his own account. They broke up in 1978, at the peak of their musical powers.  Trending Stories Watch Ariana Grande, Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro Take Over ‘The Tonight Show’ U2 Sound Revitalized on ‘Carnaval de Luz’ Del Casher, Guitarist Who Invented the Wah-Wah Pedal, Dead at 88 Russell Brand Sentenced to More Than 10 Years in Prison After Rape Conviction

Lloyd moved on to sharp solo albums like 1979’s Alchemy and 1986’s Field of Fire. He also wrote and co-produced the dBs’ 1978 debut single, “I Thought You Wanted To Know.” Television’s short-lived 1992 reunion resulted in a low-key self-titled album, with Lloyd shining in gems like “1880 or So” and “No Glamour for Willi.” (They played sporadic shows in the 2000s, but Lloyd left for good in 2007.) He joined the Cleveland proto-punks Rocket from the Tombs, in the place of their original guitarist Peter Laughner— ironic, since Laughner was the guy who briefly replaced him in Television in 1975. He was a longtime foil for the ace Nineties singer-songwriter Matthew Sweet, especially on his 1991 breakthrough Girlfriend, where the other lead guitarist was another CBGB legend, Robert Quine. Lloyd brought his unique sound to “Divine Intervention,” “I’ve Been Waiting,” “Falling,” and the 1995 MTV hit “Sick of Myself.” In the video, Lloyd plays the solo from his hospital bed, after crashing his car.

But he cleaned up and kept gigging the rest of his life — the fact that he lived to be 75 is one of his most surprising achievements. As he shrugged in his memoir, “I’ve been clinically dead a couple times, so what difference does it make to me? I like experience.” In 2002, Television reunited for their first NYC gigs in a decade. I’ll never forget the boyish mischief all over his face as he ripped through evergreens like “Venus,” “O Mi Amore,” and a wonderfully trippy “Marquee Moon.” That sense of mischief and adventure lives on in everything Richard Lloyd ever played — and that’s why his guiding light still shines on.

#3380. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

#3379. Instagram launches Edits for Mac with multi-track video editing and 4K exports

Instagram users can now download a Mac version of Edits, the company’s free video editing app, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, direct publishing to Instagram, and 4K exports. Here are the details.

Instagram is launching Edits on desktop today, bringing its free video editing app to Mac with a larger workspace, more precise editing controls, and customizable keyboard shortcuts that can match those of other video editors.

Like Edits on mobile, Instagram says its desktop counterpart will receive weekly updates and is asking users for feedback to help shape future improvements.

A lot of creators have described the same moment to us: a project gets too big for your phone. You’ve got a dozen clips going, you’re trying to land a cut on the exact beat, and your thumb covers the part of the timeline you need to see. Your work is growing, and your tools should grow with it. We’re expanding Edits to take on your most ambitious projects on desktop.

One particularly interesting feature of the new desktop app is the ability to publish videos directly to Instagram, with support for native features such as tagging, location, and trial reels.

Instagram adds that it is expanding Edits to support “multiple aspect ratios (horizontal and vertical), with 4K watermark-free export, so you can easily share to any platform, or use Edits for personal projects.”

As for the actual editing tools, Edits for desktop makes basic operations like splitting, cutting, and trimming videos easier, while also offering a full multi-track timeline, keyframes for transitions, precise audio waveforms, and advanced color grading tools such as color wheels, curves, and log conversions.

Users can also import their own LUTs and fonts, customize keyboard shortcuts, and access Instagram’s licensed audio library.

Instagram says saved audio and text styles from the mobile app are already available on desktop. However, the ability to seamlessly edit the same project across Mac and mobile is still in development.

Instagram’s desktop Edits app also offers unlimited automatic captions with support for multiple languages, as well as hundreds of sound and video effects, all for free.

#3378. Riz Ahmed Boards Elham Ehsas’ Short Film ‘Forgotten Spaceman’ About Afghanistan’s First Astronaut

EXCLUSIVE: Riz Ahmed has come on board Forgotten Spaceman, Elham Ehsas’ short film about Abdul Ahad Momand, Afghanistan’s first and only astronaut.

Ahmed is now an executive producer on the documentary film, which counts Ken Loach’s Sixteen Films among its producers. The short’s festival run has included Locarno, Toronto and London’s LFF. It has just won Best Documentary at the Aesthetica Short Film Festival and is nominated for Best British Short Film at the forthcoming 2026 British Independent Film Awards.

Ahmed previously won the Academy Award for Best Live Action Short Film in 2022 for The Long Goodbye, which he starred in, co-wrote and produced. Related Stories Documentary IDFA Announces Competition Lineups, Adds 'Musk' And Elizabeth Holmes Documentary 'You Can See Everything' Documentary IDFA Announces Forum Lineup: Projects From Wang Bing, Rachel Leah Jones, Vitaly Mansky, Juanjo Pereira, Liang Zhao & More

“Forgotten Spaceman begins with the extraordinary story of Afghanistan’s first astronaut, but Elham makes it deeply personal through his own family connection and experience of displacement,” Ahmed said. “It offers a perspective on Afghanistan beyond the headlines, and it’s been incredible to see the film resonate with audiences around the world. I’m proud to support Elham and the team as its journey continues.” Watch on Deadline

The film follows Momand’s 1988 trip to space, as part of a Soviet mission. It captures his story and, in the process, that of Afghanistan during this era.

Ehsas’ previous short, Yellow, was BAFTA-nominated and shortlisted for the Academy Awards in 2024. He wrote and directed Forgotten Spaceman, which also tells the story of his own family, his father having been the first person to interview Momand when he returned to Earth.

“Having Riz come on board is a real honor,” the filmmaker said. “He’s spent his career championing stories that might slip through the cracks, elevating distinctive voices and histories the world might otherwise miss. For him to put his weight behind this piece of Afghan history means more than I can put into words.”

Ahmed joins an executive producer team that includes Jack Thomas-O’Brien of Ken Loach and Rebecca O’Brien’s Sixteen Films, Catherine Tschaepe, Sharib Khan and Vikas Kumar of Khan & Kumar Media and Shruti Ganguly, Priya Giri Desai and Megha Kadakia of Prism Entertainment.

Forgotten Spaceman is produced by Elham Ehsas of Foreigner Films and Lorraine Bhattachary of MonoFilm Productions, with Dheeraj Agnihotri serving as Associate Producer. International sales and festival strategy are handled by María Vera of Kino Rebelde.

The Oscar and BAFTA qualified film’s festival run is continuing with screenings at International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam, among others.

#3376. WhatsApp adds shareable event invites and a new Events hub

WhatsApp is rolling out an update to Events just in time for holiday get-togethers. Guests can open an invite link, see the event details, and RSVP without creating a WhatsApp account or downloading the app.

When you create an event, you can add a cover photo and share the invite link by text or email. WhatsApp also gives you the option to share a QR code.

WhatsApp says your phone number is hidden from guests you don’t know, and “guests without a WhatsApp account will only see the event address after they RSVP.”

You could already create events in WhatsApp group chats and one-on-one conversations.

With this update, WhatsApp is adding a dedicated Events section in Settings where you can create invites, manage RSVPs, and see past and upcoming events you’ve organized or been invited to.

You can also set custom reminders and give guests the option to bring a plus-one.

WhatsApp says the updated Events feature will roll out to everyone over the next few weeks.

#3375. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.
